prompt: A request states what was tried and what happened, in detail, and has gone unanswered for two days. Nothing about it is impolite and its detail is accurate. What is it most likely missing?
optionA: More detail about what was tried
optionB: A polite opening and closing
optionC: A deadline by which an answer is needed
optionD: What the sender expected instead, without which nobody can tell whether the behaviour is even wrong
correctAnswerText: What the sender expected instead, without which nobody can tell whether the behaviour is even wrong
explanation: A precise account of behaviour is not yet a question if the reader cannot see what would count as an answer. Adding detail to a report that is already detailed does not supply the one thing that is absent.

prompt: Four comments are made on the same piece of work. Which one tells the author what to change?
optionA: "The function name says it validates, but it also saves — consider splitting the two."
optionB: "This function is doing a bit much, I think."
optionC: "Good effort overall, though it could be tidier."
optionD: "I would have written this differently."
correctAnswerText: "The function name says it validates, but it also saves — consider splitting the two."
explanation: Only the first names what is wrong and what to do about it. The other three are polite and leave the author guessing, which is what makes actionability rather than tone the criterion.

prompt: A reviewer writes: "Rename this variable to itemCount." The author does so and the reviewer then objects that the underlying problem remains. The instruction was followed exactly. What was wrong with the feedback?
optionA: It was too blunt in tone
optionB: It named a specific variable rather than describing the pattern
optionC: It gave a direction without its reason, so the author could not tell what the change was meant to achieve
optionD: Nothing; the author should have asked what was meant
correctAnswerText: It gave a direction without its reason, so the author could not tell what the change was meant to achieve
explanation: The change was made exactly as asked and did not achieve what the reviewer wanted, which means the instruction and the intent had come apart. Feedback carrying its reason lets an author reach the intent even when the specific instruction is imperfect.

prompt: Instructions read: "Clear the cache and restart the service." A reader restarted the service without clearing anything. Which wording permitted that?
optionA: "Clear", which could mean several things
optionB: Nothing did; the reader skipped a step the instruction states plainly
optionC: "The cache", which is not identified
optionD: "And", which could join two alternatives
correctAnswerText: Nothing did; the reader skipped a step the instruction states plainly
explanation: Both steps are stated and neither is optional, so this is a reader error rather than a text one. Being able to say that the text is not at fault is as much part of the skill as locating a fault when there is one.

prompt: Instructions read: "Copy the configuration file into the application directory and edit it to add your key." A reader edited the original file instead of the copy. Every step in the instruction is present and in the right order. Which wording permitted that?
optionA: "Copy", which could mean move
optionB: "The application directory", which is not identified
optionC: "Your key", which is not explained
optionD: "It" does not say which of the two files, and the original was the last one clearly named
correctAnswerText: "It" does not say which of the two files, and the original was the last one clearly named
explanation: The reader's action is a reasonable reading of the pronoun, which is the only part of the sentence that leaves two candidates. The other imprecisions are real and would have produced different mistakes.

prompt: Six readers follow the same instruction and four of them do the same unintended thing. What does the pattern tell you, and what does it not?
optionA: That the wording permits their reading; it does not tell you which words, and it does not show the readers were careless
optionB: That the four readers were careless
optionC: That the instruction is grammatically incorrect
optionD: That the two who got it right misread it
correctAnswerText: That the wording permits their reading; it does not tell you which words, and it does not show the readers were careless
explanation: Several people independently reaching the same wrong reading is strong evidence that the reading is available in the text. Which words permit it still has to be found, and that a minority read it as intended shows only that the text admits both.

prompt: An instruction has been followed wrongly once in two years. Rewriting it would take an hour and would need every translated version updated. Should it be rewritten?
optionA: Yes; any wording that has ever been misread should be rewritten
optionB: No; one misreading in two years is within tolerance
optionC: It depends on the cost of the wrong action; a single rare misreading of something harmless is not worth the cascade, and one that loses data is
optionD: Yes; clarity is always worth an hour
correctAnswerText: It depends on the cost of the wrong action; a single rare misreading of something harmless is not worth the cascade, and one that loses data is
explanation: Whether to repair wording is not settled by how often it misleads alone — what matters is what happens when it does. A rule that fires on any single misreading ignores the cost of changing things that many people depend on.

prompt: A writer says their instruction is fine because it is technically correct, and readers are getting it wrong. Is technical correctness a defence?
optionA: Yes; a correct instruction cannot be at fault
optionB: No; an instruction exists to produce an action, so one that reliably produces the wrong action has failed whatever it technically says
optionC: No; instructions are never technically correct
optionD: Yes, provided the readers were not the intended audience
correctAnswerText: No; an instruction exists to produce an action, so one that reliably produces the wrong action has failed whatever it technically says
explanation: Correctness settles what the words mean and not whether they work. Text that is defensible word by word and reliably misread is a failure of the same kind as a program that is legal and does the wrong thing.

prompt: A message reads: "The report is late." The named defect is that it does not say what is needed from the reader. The message is short, civil and accurate. Which rewrite removes that defect?
optionA: "Unfortunately the report is running late, and I apologise for the delay."
optionB: "The report is late because the figures have not arrived."
optionC: "The report is late. This has happened twice this month."
optionD: "The report is late; could you send me the figures today so I can finish it?"
correctAnswerText: "The report is late; could you send me the figures today so I can finish it?"
explanation: Only the first says what the reader should do. The second improves tone, the third supplies a cause and the fourth adds context — all genuine improvements that leave the named defect exactly where it was.

prompt: A message reads: "Please review this when you can." The named defect is that it gives no deadline. Which rewrite removes that defect and introduces no new one?
optionA: "Please review this by Thursday; let me know if that is not possible."
optionB: "Please review this urgently."
optionC: "Please review this as soon as possible."
optionD: "Please review this by Thursday or I will have to escalate."
correctAnswerText: "Please review this by Thursday; let me know if that is not possible."
explanation: A date is what a deadline is, and offering a route to say no keeps the request civil. "Urgently" and "as soon as possible" are as unfixed as the original, and the fourth attaches a threat, which is a new defect.

prompt: A message reads: "The change broke the build." The named defect is that it names no change and no failure. Which rewrite removes exactly that defect?
optionA: "Someone's change broke the build and it needs fixing quickly."
optionB: "The build is broken; please look into it when you can."
optionC: "The change to the date parser broke the build: the timezone tests now fail."
optionD: "The change to the date parser broke the build."
correctAnswerText: "The change to the date parser broke the build: the timezone tests now fail."
explanation: Both halves of the defect have to go, and only the first supplies the change and the failure. The last option repairs one half and leaves the other, which is the most tempting wrong answer because it plainly improves the message.

prompt: A message has two defects: it is ambiguous about which file, and it is curt. Only one rewrite is possible before the message must be sent. Which defect should be repaired?
optionA: The curtness, because tone affects whether the message is acted on at all
optionB: The ambiguity, because it can cause the wrong action, whereas curtness costs goodwill
optionC: Neither; a message with two defects should not be sent
optionD: Both are equally serious, so either choice is defensible
correctAnswerText: The ambiguity, because it can cause the wrong action, whereas curtness costs goodwill
explanation: One defect risks the wrong file being touched and the other risks mild offence, and only the first has a consequence the message exists to prevent. Ranking defects by what they cause is what makes a single repair a decision rather than a guess.

prompt: A rewrite removes the named defect and makes the message twice as long. When is that a bad trade?
optionA: Always; a longer message is always worse
optionB: Never; removing a defect is always worth any length
optionC: When the original was already grammatical
optionD: When the length puts the essential part where a hurried reader will not reach it
correctAnswerText: When the length puts the essential part where a hurried reader will not reach it
explanation: Length matters only through its effect on whether the message is read and acted on, so the question is where the important part now sits. A longer message that leads with what matters costs almost nothing.

prompt: A decision must be recorded so that people who join later can find it, and it must reach four named people today. A written record is required and immediacy is not. Which form fits?
optionA: A written note in the shared document, with a message pointing the four people at it
optionB: A call with the four people
optionC: A message to the four people only
optionD: A note in the shared document only
correctAnswerText: A written note in the shared document, with a message pointing the four people at it
explanation: Both constraints have to be met, and each single-channel option meets one. A call leaves no record, a message reaches the four and is unfindable later, and a document alone does not reach them today.

prompt: A production system is failing now, three people must act within minutes, and a record is wanted afterwards. Which form fits, and in what order?
optionA: Write the record first, so nothing is forgotten
optionB: Write the record only, since it reaches everyone eventually
optionC: Reach the three immediately by whatever is fastest, then write the record once the failure is handled
optionD: Reach the three immediately, and treat the messages as the record
correctAnswerText: Reach the three immediately by whatever is fastest, then write the record once the failure is handled
explanation: Both needs are real and one of them is urgent, so they are met in sequence rather than traded off. Treating the scattered messages as the record satisfies the letter of the requirement and leaves nothing anybody can find.

prompt: A question needs an answer from one person, and the answer will matter to a team of twenty later. Asking privately is faster. What does each choice cost?
optionA: Privately costs nothing, since the answer can be shared afterwards
optionB: Privately is faster and the answer reaches nobody else; publicly is slower and the answer is there when the next person asks
optionC: Publicly costs nothing, since it reaches everyone
optionD: They are equivalent, since one person answers either way
correctAnswerText: Privately is faster and the answer reaches nobody else; publicly is slower and the answer is there when the next person asks
explanation: The two differ in what happens after the answer arrives. Sharing afterwards is possible and usually does not happen, which is the cost the private route actually carries.

prompt: A message must reach someone who is unavailable for two days, and the matter cannot wait that long. What follows about the form?
optionA: Send it by every channel at once, so it arrives as soon as they return
optionB: Send it and wait, since the message has been delivered
optionC: Send it to the whole team, so somebody sees it
optionD: The form cannot solve it; the choice is to escalate to somebody available or to accept the delay, and that decision has to be made explicitly
correctAnswerText: The form cannot solve it; the choice is to escalate to somebody available or to accept the delay, and that decision has to be made explicitly
explanation: When no channel meets the constraints, choosing a channel is not the decision to be made. Sending and waiting satisfies the form and not the need, and broadcasting to everyone is an escalation made without deciding to escalate.

prompt: Which of these is a well-formed C declaration?
optionA: count;
optionB: int count;
optionC: count = 0;
optionD: var count;
correctAnswerText: int count;
explanation: A C declaration states a type before the name. A bare name, or an assignment with no type, is valid in some other languages and not here.

prompt: A C program contains: int total = 5; total = 2.7; What type does total hold afterwards?
optionA: double, because a fractional value was assigned
optionB: int, and the program refuses to compile
optionC: Whichever type the most recent assignment used
optionD: int, still; the fractional part is discarded on assignment
correctAnswerText: int, still; the fractional part is discarded on assignment
explanation: A name's type is fixed at its declaration and no assignment changes it. The value is converted to fit, silently losing the fraction, which is why nothing is reported.

prompt: What does the declaration int a, b; do?
optionA: Declares two variables, both of type int
optionB: Declares one variable whose name is a, b
optionC: Declares a as int and leaves b untyped
optionD: Is not valid; each name needs its own declaration
correctAnswerText: Declares two variables, both of type int
explanation: One type may introduce several names separated by commas, and every name takes that type. Neither leaving one untyped nor requiring separate lines is the rule.

prompt: A C program uses the name total without any declaration of it anywhere. What happens?
optionA: The program runs and total starts at zero
optionB: The program runs and total holds an unpredictable value
optionC: The program does not compile; C requires a declaration before use
optionD: The compiler infers the type from the first assignment
correctAnswerText: The program does not compile; C requires a declaration before use
explanation: A missing declaration is caught before the program runs at all. That is different from a declared variable never assigned to, which does compile and does hold an unpredictable value.

prompt: A C program contains printf("%d", x) with no declaration of x. What is the problem?
optionA: printf cannot print whole numbers
optionB: x must be declared, with a type, before it can be used
optionC: The specifier should be %s for a variable
optionD: Nothing; x is created by being used
correctAnswerText: x must be declared, with a type, before it can be used
explanation: Every name in C needs a declaration that fixes its type before any use of it. Being created on first use is how some other languages work and is exactly the habit this catches.

prompt: A variable is declared as int. Which value can it hold exactly?
optionB: "hello"
optionC: 'a' and 'b' together
explanation: A whole-number type holds whole numbers, negative ones included. A fraction loses its fractional part, and text is a different kind of thing entirely.

prompt: A variable is declared as char. What can it hold?
optionA: A single character
optionB: A word of any length
optionC: A whole number of any size
optionD: A fractional value
correctAnswerText: A single character
explanation: A char holds one character. Storing a word needs an array of them, which is why text in C is handled differently from a single letter.

prompt: A variable declared as int is given the value 3.9. What does it hold?
optionD: Nothing; the assignment is refused
explanation: Conversion into a whole-number type discards the fraction rather than rounding it, so 3.9 becomes 3. Nothing is reported, which is what makes the loss easy to miss.

prompt: A whole-number type is given a value far beyond the largest it can represent. What happens?
optionA: The program stops with an error
optionB: The value wraps to something within range, and nothing is reported
optionC: The type grows to accommodate the value
optionD: The value is stored exactly, since whole numbers have no limit
correctAnswerText: The value wraps to something within range, and nothing is reported
explanation: A C whole-number type has a fixed size and therefore a fixed range, and exceeding it produces a value inside the range rather than a complaint. Assuming such types are unbounded is a habit brought from languages where they are.

prompt: Which specifier prints a value declared as int?
optionA: %f
optionB: %c
optionC: %s
optionD: %d
correctAnswerText: %d
explanation: Each specifier names a type, and %d is the one for a whole number. Using the wrong one does not convert the value; it reads the same bytes as though they were a different type.

prompt: A program declares int x = 5 and then calls printf("%f", x). What happens?
optionA: It compiles and prints something meaningless; the mismatch is not corrected
optionB: It prints 5.000000, converting automatically
optionC: It refuses to compile because the types differ
optionD: It prints 5 and ignores the specifier
correctAnswerText: It compiles and prints something meaningless; the mismatch is not corrected
explanation: The specifier decides how the bytes are read, and nothing converts the value to match it. That a mismatch produces nonsense rather than an error is what makes it hard for a beginner to explain.

prompt: Which of these pairs a value with a specifier that matches it?
optionA: an int printed with %f
optionB: a char printed with %s
optionC: a double printed with %f
optionD: a double printed with %d
correctAnswerText: a double printed with %f
explanation: A specifier has to name the type it is given. %s expects text ending in a terminator rather than a single character, and the two remaining pairs each read a value as though it were a different type.

prompt: A program prints a double using %d and the output is a large unrelated number. The value stored is correct. What happened?
optionA: The value was corrupted when it was assigned
optionB: The specifier read the value as though it were a whole number, so the bytes were interpreted wrongly
optionC: The value was rounded to the nearest whole number
optionD: printf converted the value and lost precision
correctAnswerText: The specifier read the value as though it were a whole number, so the bytes were interpreted wrongly
explanation: The stored value is fine and the reading of it is not — a specifier is an instruction about interpretation, not a request to convert. Rounding would have produced a plausible number rather than an unrelated one.

prompt: A C program declares int total; and prints it without assigning anything. What is printed?
optionB: Nothing
optionC: An error message about an unassigned variable
optionD: Whatever happened to be in that memory — an unpredictable value
correctAnswerText: Whatever happened to be in that memory — an unpredictable value
explanation: Declaring reserves space and does not clear it, so the variable holds whatever was there. Assuming zero is the belief that makes accumulator faults invisible.

prompt: A program that sums values into an undeclared starting total gives a different answer on different runs. What accounts for that?
optionA: The total began at whatever was in memory, which differs from run to run
optionB: The values being summed differ from run to run
optionC: The addition is unreliable in C
optionD: The compiler optimises the loop differently each time
correctAnswerText: The total began at whatever was in memory, which differs from run to run
explanation: An unassigned variable does not merely hold a wrong value; it holds an unpredictable one, so the same data gives different answers. That variability is the signature of an initialisation fault rather than an arithmetic one.

prompt: A C program prints the result of 17 / 5, where both values are whole numbers. What is printed?
explanation: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number with the remainder discarded, so 3.4 becomes 3. Rounding would give 4, which is why an operand pair whose fraction exceeds a half is what separates the two rules.

prompt: A C program computes 9 / 2 and stores the result in a double. What does the double hold?
optionA: 4.5, because the destination is a fractional type
optionB: 4.0, because the division truncated before the value was stored
optionC: 4, and the type of the destination is irrelevant
optionD: 5.0, because the result is rounded on conversion
correctAnswerText: 4.0, because the division truncated before the value was stored
explanation: The division happens first, between two whole numbers, and produces 4; storing that in a fractional type gives 4.0. What is lost before the assignment cannot be recovered by the assignment.

prompt: A C program computes 7 / 2.0. What is the result and its type?
optionA: 3, a whole number
optionB: 4, a whole number
optionC: 3.5, but stored as a whole number
optionD: 3.5, a fractional value
correctAnswerText: 3.5, a fractional value
explanation: Because one operand is fractional, the other is converted before the division, so nothing is truncated. Writing 2 rather than 2.0 is the whole difference.

prompt: A C program computes 1 + 7 / 2, with all values written as whole numbers. What is the result?
explanation: The division runs first and truncates to 3, and adding 1 gives 4. Working the expression out in fractions throughout and then truncating would give 4 as well by coincidence here — but answering 4.5 shows the truncation was not applied at all.

prompt: A C program computes (double)(sum / count), where sum and count are both whole numbers, and the result is always a whole number however the values are chosen. The conversion to double is present and correct. Why does it not help?
optionA: The conversion should be applied to the result of the assignment instead
optionB: A double cannot represent the fractional part of a division
optionC: The division has already truncated by the time the conversion happens
optionD: sum and count should be declared as long rather than int
correctAnswerText: The division has already truncated by the time the conversion happens
explanation: The brackets place the conversion after the division, so it converts a value from which the fraction has already gone. Converting one operand before dividing is what changes the arithmetic.

prompt: A C read must be told two things about where the value goes. What are they?
optionA: What type to expect, and how many characters to read
optionB: What type to expect, and the location to put it in
optionC: The location to put it in, and a default value
optionD: Only the location; the type is worked out from the input
correctAnswerText: What type to expect, and the location to put it in
explanation: A read has to know how to interpret what arrives and where to place the result, and neither can be inferred. Nothing about the typed characters tells the program what type was intended.

prompt: A C read expecting a whole number is given text that is not a number. What happens to the variable?
optionA: It is set to zero
optionB: The program stops with an error
optionC: The text is converted to the number of characters it contains
optionD: It is left as it was; the read does not store anything
correctAnswerText: It is left as it was; the read does not store anything
explanation: A failed read reports its failure and leaves the destination untouched, so the variable keeps whatever it had — which may be unpredictable if it was never assigned. Nothing halts, which is why the failure has to be checked for.

prompt: A program reads a number and then behaves as though a completely different value had been typed. The read itself reports success, and the variable was declared but never assigned before the read. What is the likely fault?
optionA: The read was given the variable rather than its location, so the value went somewhere else
optionB: The variable was declared with the wrong type
optionC: The input contained characters that could not be converted
optionD: The value was correct and the later arithmetic is wrong
correctAnswerText: The read was given the variable rather than its location, so the value went somewhere else
explanation: A read reporting success while the variable holds something unrelated points at where the value was sent rather than at what was read. The variable never having been assigned is what makes the leftover value look like a plausible reading.

prompt: A C program declares int a[3] = {10, 20, 30} and prints a[1]. What is printed?
explanation: Positions run from zero, so a[1] is the second item and 20 is printed. Reading a[0] would give the first item, which is what counting from one produces.

prompt: An array is declared with size 8. Which positions are valid?
optionA: 1 to 8
optionB: 0 to 7
optionC: 0 to 8
optionD: 1 to 7
correctAnswerText: 0 to 7
explanation: A declared size of 8 gives eight positions beginning at zero, so the last is 7. Using the size itself as a position is the single commonest way to run past the end.

prompt: A loop over an array declared with size 5 runs from 0 to 5 inclusive and the program produces a wrong total. It compiles without complaint and runs to completion. What is wrong?
optionA: The array should have been declared with size 6
optionB: The loop should start at 1 rather than 0
optionC: The total was not initialised before the loop
optionD: The loop reads one position past the end, adding whatever happens to be there
correctAnswerText: The loop reads one position past the end, adding whatever happens to be there
explanation: Compiling and completing rules out anything the compiler would catch, and the extra pass reads memory beyond the array. Enlarging the array would remove the symptom while leaving the loop wrong for every other array.

prompt: A C program reads a position beyond the end of an array. What does it do?
optionA: It reads whatever is in that memory and carries on
optionB: It stops with an out-of-range error
optionC: It returns zero for any position beyond the end
optionD: It refuses to compile
correctAnswerText: It reads whatever is in that memory and carries on
explanation: Nothing checks the position, so the read succeeds and produces meaningless data. The absence of a check is exactly what distinguishes C from languages that report this.

prompt: A program with an out-of-range array read appears to work correctly for weeks and then produces nonsense. What explains both?
optionA: The array grew over time and eventually ran out of space
optionB: The fault appears only when the program runs for a long time
optionC: The memory beyond the array happened to hold harmless values, until something else was placed there
optionD: The compiler removed the check and later restored it
correctAnswerText: The memory beyond the array happened to hold harmless values, until something else was placed there
explanation: An unchecked read produces whatever is in that memory, and that depends on what else the program is doing. Appearing to work is not evidence the access is valid, which is what makes this class of fault so long-lived.

prompt: A program writes one position beyond an array and a different, unrelated variable changes value. The write reports nothing and the program continues. What happened?
optionA: The two variables were declared with the same name
optionB: The write went into memory belonging to something else, which is not detected
optionC: The compiler placed the two variables in the same location deliberately
optionD: The array automatically grew into the neighbouring variable
correctAnswerText: The write went into memory belonging to something else, which is not detected
explanation: Writing past the end puts data wherever that position lands, and neighbouring variables are often exactly what is there. Nothing reports it, which is why the symptom appears somewhere entirely unrelated to the fault.

prompt: How many positions are needed to store the text "cat" in C?
optionC: It depends on the machine
explanation: Three characters need three positions, and the terminator that marks the end needs one more. Forgetting it is what produces text that runs on past its end.

prompt: An array is declared with size 5 and the text "hello" is copied into it. What is the problem?
optionA: There is no room for the terminator, so the text has no end marker
optionB: There is no problem; five characters fit in five positions
optionC: The text is one character too long and will be truncated
optionD: The array will grow by one position automatically
correctAnswerText: There is no room for the terminator, so the text has no end marker
explanation: The five letters fill every position and leave nowhere for the terminator. Nothing truncates and nothing grows — the terminator is simply written past the end, or omitted, and the text has no recognised end.

prompt: A program prints a piece of text and produces the expected characters followed by a run of meaningless ones. The characters themselves were copied correctly. What is wrong?
optionA: The array is too large, so the extra positions are printed
optionB: The wrong specifier was used to print it
optionC: The terminator is missing, so printing continues past the end of the text
optionD: The characters were copied one position too far along
correctAnswerText: The terminator is missing, so printing continues past the end of the text
explanation: Correct characters followed by rubbish is the signature of a missing end marker: printing stops at a terminator and there is none. An oversized array is harmless, because the terminator would still stop the printing.

prompt: A C program runs: int x = 10; double y = x / 4; printf("%f", y); What is printed?
explanation: Both operands of the division are whole numbers, so the fraction is discarded before y is assigned and 2.000000 is printed. Declaring y as a fractional type changes how the value is stored and shown, not how it was computed.

prompt: Two fragments differ only in one declaration: one has int a = 7, double b = 2; the other has double a = 7, int b = 2. Both compute a / b. Both compile and both produce the same answer. Why?
optionA: Because 7 divides by 2 exactly, so the types make no difference
optionB: Because the compiler chooses the fractional type in both cases regardless
optionC: Because the result is stored in the same type in both fragments
optionD: Either declaration makes one operand fractional, so the other is converted before the division
correctAnswerText: Either declaration makes one operand fractional, so the other is converted before the division
explanation: Conversion happens when the two operands differ, and which of the two is fractional does not matter. Had both been whole numbers the answer would differ, which is what makes the declaration the thing being measured.

prompt: A C program compiles without warnings, runs to completion, and prints a wrong total. What does the absence of any error message tell you?
optionA: Nothing about correctness; a C program can be entirely legal and produce the wrong answer
optionB: That the fault must be in the input rather than the program
optionC: That the fault must be a truncation, since nothing else is silent
optionD: That the compiler failed to check the program properly
correctAnswerText: Nothing about correctness; a C program can be entirely legal and produce the wrong answer
explanation: Compiling checks that the program is well formed and says nothing about what it computes. Truncation is one silent cause among several, so the absence of a message narrows nothing.

prompt: A program sums an array and prints a total far larger than any plausible sum. The array values and the loop bounds are both correct. Which silent fault fits?
optionA: A truncation lost part of each value
optionB: The array was declared too small
optionC: The running total was never assigned a starting value, so the sum began from rubbish
optionD: The output specifier did not match the type
correctAnswerText: The running total was never assigned a starting value, so the sum began from rubbish
explanation: A total far too large points at a starting value that was never set, since truncation can only lose value and correct bounds rule out reading extra items. Distinguishing the two silent causes is what the symptom is for.

prompt: A C program averages whole-number marks and always reports a whole number. Where is the precision lost?
optionA: In the printing, because the specifier is for whole numbers
optionB: In the division, because both the total and the count are whole numbers
optionC: In the addition, because whole numbers cannot hold fractions
optionD: In the declaration of the marks, which should be fractional
correctAnswerText: In the division, because both the total and the count are whole numbers
explanation: Addition of whole numbers loses nothing, and printing cannot restore what is gone. The division is where a fraction would first arise and is where it is discarded.

prompt: A programmer changes the average variable from int to double and the answer is still a whole number. The change was made correctly and the program recompiled. Why did it not work?
optionA: double cannot hold the fractional part of an average
optionB: The variable needs to be declared before the marks are read
optionC: The output specifier still prints whole numbers
optionD: The division still has two whole-number operands, so the fraction is gone before the assignment
correctAnswerText: The division still has two whole-number operands, so the fraction is gone before the assignment
explanation: Changing where a value is stored does nothing about how it was computed. The fraction has to survive the division to be worth storing, which means converting an operand rather than the result.

prompt: Three fixes are proposed for a whole-number average: store the result in a double, print it with a fractional specifier, or convert one operand before dividing. Which works, and why do the others not?
optionA: Converting an operand before dividing; the other two act after the fraction has already been discarded
optionB: Storing in a double; the destination type governs the arithmetic
optionC: Printing with a fractional specifier; the value was always fractional
optionD: All three work, since each involves a fractional type
correctAnswerText: Converting an operand before dividing; the other two act after the fraction has already been discarded
explanation: The order of events settles it: the division happens first, and only something that changes what the division sees can preserve the fraction. Both other fixes involve a fractional type and arrive too late to matter.

prompt: A calculation divides by 100 early and multiplies by 100 later, using whole numbers throughout. The final answer is wrong even though the two operations should cancel. Why?
optionA: The multiplication overflowed the type
optionB: Dividing and multiplying by the same value never cancel in C
optionC: The division discarded the fraction, and multiplying afterwards cannot restore what is no longer there
optionD: The operations were applied in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: The division discarded the fraction, and multiplying afterwards cannot restore what is no longer there
explanation: The two operations do cancel in arithmetic and not in whole-number arithmetic, because the first loses information. Reordering them — multiplying first — would keep the value intact, which is why the order is worth noticing.

prompt: Whole-number arithmetic is faster and truncates; fractional arithmetic keeps the fraction and costs more. When is the whole-number choice wrong?
optionA: Never; whole numbers are always preferable when the inputs are whole
optionB: Whenever the discarded fraction affects the answer that is actually needed — a count of items is fine, an average is not
optionC: Always; fractional types should be used throughout
optionD: Whenever the values are large, since large values lose more
correctAnswerText: Whenever the discarded fraction affects the answer that is actually needed — a count of items is fine, an average is not
explanation: The choice depends on what the result means rather than on what the inputs are. Counting produces a whole number by nature; averaging produces one only by accident, and the size of the values has nothing to do with it.

prompt: A C program computes -7 / 2 with whole numbers and prints -3. A programmer expected -4. The same program prints 3 for 7 / 2, which they expected. What rule is in force?
optionA: Whole-number division rounds to the nearest value
optionB: Whole-number division moves down to the next lower whole number
optionC: Negative division is undefined and the result cannot be relied on
optionD: Whole-number division discards the fraction, moving toward zero in both directions
correctAnswerText: Whole-number division discards the fraction, moving toward zero in both directions
explanation: Discarding the fraction from -3.5 gives -3, and from 3.5 gives 3 — both toward zero. Moving down would give -4, which is what some other languages do, and is exactly why the positive case alone cannot reveal the rule.

prompt: A whole-number counter increases past the largest value its type can hold. What happens next?
optionA: It wraps around to a large negative value, silently
optionB: It stops increasing and stays at the maximum
optionC: The program stops with an overflow error
optionD: The type widens automatically to hold the value
correctAnswerText: It wraps around to a large negative value, silently
explanation: A fixed-size type has no room beyond its maximum, and the next increase produces a value at the other end of the range. Nothing reports it, so a counter can become negative while the program carries on as though nothing happened.

prompt: A C program divides by a value read from input. What should be checked before the division, and what happens if it is not?
optionA: That the value is positive; a negative divisor gives an unpredictable result
optionB: Nothing; C returns zero when dividing by zero
optionC: That the value is not zero; dividing by zero is not caught by the compiler and stops the program at run time
optionD: That the value fits the type; the compiler checks the rest
correctAnswerText: That the value is not zero; dividing by zero is not caught by the compiler and stops the program at run time
explanation: A zero divisor is the one case the arithmetic cannot produce an answer for, and nothing before the program runs can know the input. Negative divisors are perfectly well defined, and no value is quietly returned.

prompt: Two C faults behave differently: dividing by zero stops the program, while writing past an array does not. Which is more dangerous in a program that runs unattended, and why?
optionA: The division, because a stopped program produces nothing at all
optionB: The array write, because the program carries on producing results that are quietly wrong
optionC: They are equally dangerous, since both are faults
optionD: The array write, because it is harder to find in the code
correctAnswerText: The array write, because the program carries on producing results that are quietly wrong
explanation: A program that stops announces its own failure and whoever reads the log finds out. A silent wrong write leaves plausible output that is acted on, which is the more costly outcome even though it looks like the milder one.

prompt: A program works correctly for every input it has been tested with, all of them small positive whole numbers. Which untested inputs are most likely to expose a type limit?
optionA: Values in the middle of the tested range
optionB: Repeated values, since repetition accumulates error
optionC: Values with many digits, since long numbers are harder to store
optionD: Zero, negative values, and values near the largest the type can hold
correctAnswerText: Zero, negative values, and values near the largest the type can hold
explanation: Type limits show at the boundaries of what a type can represent and at the values arithmetic treats specially. Repetition and digit count are not what a fixed-size whole-number type is sensitive to.

prompt: The same averaging algorithm is written in C and in Python. Both are correct transcriptions of each other. On whole-number input they disagree. Why?
optionA: C truncates the division of two whole numbers; Python's single slash produces a fractional result
optionB: C is faster, so it rounds differently under time pressure
optionC: Python stores whole numbers with more precision
optionD: The transcription must be wrong, since correct transcriptions agree
correctAnswerText: C truncates the division of two whole numbers; Python's single slash produces a fractional result
explanation: The difference is in what the division operator means for two whole numbers, which is a property of the language rather than of the algorithm. A faithful transcription can still behave differently when the two languages define an operator differently.

prompt: The same loop reads one position past the end of a collection, in C and in Python. What happens in each?
optionA: Both stop with an error
optionB: Both read whatever is there and carry on
optionC: C reads whatever is there and carries on; Python stops with an error
optionD: C stops with an error; Python returns an empty value
correctAnswerText: C reads whatever is there and carries on; Python stops with an error
explanation: Python checks the position and refuses; C does not check at all. The same mistake is therefore loud in one language and silent in the other, which is the difference most worth carrying between them.

prompt: A whole-number counter is increased far beyond a few billion, in C and in Python. Where do the two disagree?
optionA: Both wrap at the same point
optionB: C wraps once the type's range is exceeded; Python holds whole numbers of any size
optionC: Both hold whole numbers of any size
optionD: C holds any size; Python wraps at a fixed limit
correctAnswerText: C wraps once the type's range is exceeded; Python holds whole numbers of any size
explanation: A C whole-number type has a fixed size, while Python's grows as needed. A program transcribed from Python can therefore be correct there and quietly wrong in C on exactly the inputs that exceed the type.

prompt: A team must choose whether to prototype in Python and rewrite in C, or write in C from the start. What does the first route buy, and what does it risk?
optionA: It buys nothing; a rewrite doubles the work
optionB: It risks nothing; a faithful transcription behaves identically
optionC: It buys speed, since Python code runs faster once rewritten
optionD: It buys a working algorithm sooner, and risks a transcription that is faithful and behaves differently on division, array bounds and large values
correctAnswerText: It buys a working algorithm sooner, and risks a transcription that is faithful and behaves differently on division, array bounds and large values
explanation: Getting the algorithm right first is a genuine gain, and the risk is precisely the places where a faithful transcription is not an equivalent program. Knowing which three places those are is what makes the route usable rather than dangerous.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0) printf("A"); printf("B"); with both prints written on separate, equally indented lines. Which of them is controlled by the condition?
optionA: Both, because they are indented together
optionB: Only the first
optionC: Neither, because there are no braces
optionD: Only the second
correctAnswerText: Only the first
explanation: Without braces a conditional governs exactly one statement, which is the first. Indentation is invisible to the compiler, so lining the two up changes nothing about which is controlled.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0) { printf("A"); printf("B"); } How many statements are controlled by the condition?
optionA: One, the first only
optionB: None, because braces separate them from the condition
optionC: Two, but only if they are indented
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: Braces group statements into one block, and the whole block is what the condition governs. Indentation plays no part in either direction.

prompt: Are braces compulsory after a C conditional?
optionA: No; without them the conditional governs the single statement that follows
optionB: Yes; a conditional without braces does not compile
optionC: Yes, unless the body is on the same line
optionD: No; without them the conditional governs everything until the next blank line
correctAnswerText: No; without them the conditional governs the single statement that follows
explanation: One statement needs no braces, which is precisely why adding a second line later is such a common way to break working code. Blank lines mean nothing to the compiler.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0); printf("A"); What does the condition control?
optionA: The print, which runs only when x is positive
optionB: Nothing, and the fragment does not compile
optionC: Nothing; the semicolon is an empty statement and is the whole body
optionD: The print, which runs regardless of x
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the semicolon is an empty statement and is the whole body
explanation: A semicolon on its own is a complete, empty statement, and the conditional takes it as its body. The print then sits outside the conditional and runs every time — legal, silent and almost never what was meant.

prompt: A C fragment reads: while (i < 5); { total += i; i++; } The program never finishes and never prints anything. Why?
optionA: The braces are in the wrong place and the program does not compile
optionB: The semicolon makes the loop body empty, so nothing ever changes i
optionC: The increment is inside the braces and so never runs
optionD: The condition should have used <= rather than <
correctAnswerText: The semicolon makes the loop body empty, so nothing ever changes i
explanation: The loop repeats an empty statement forever, because nothing inside it can make the condition false. The braced block is a separate block that is never reached, which is why nothing prints either.

prompt: In C, is the condition if (3) satisfied?
optionA: No; only the value 1 counts as true
optionB: No; a condition must be a comparison
optionC: It does not compile; 3 is not a condition
optionD: Yes; any value other than zero counts as true
correctAnswerText: Yes; any value other than zero counts as true
explanation: A C condition is a number, and every non-zero value is treated as true. Requiring a comparison is a rule from other languages that C does not impose.

prompt: A variable holds the result of 2 - 6. Used directly as a C condition, is it satisfied?
optionA: Yes; the result is -4, which is not zero, so it counts as true
optionB: No; a negative result counts as false
optionC: No; only a positive result counts as true
optionD: It cannot be used as a condition without a comparison
correctAnswerText: Yes; the result is -4, which is not zero, so it counts as true
explanation: What matters is only whether the value differs from zero, so a negative result satisfies the test. Reading "true" as "positive" is the natural but wrong reading of a numeric condition.

prompt: In C, is the condition if (0) satisfied?
optionA: Yes; zero is a valid value
optionB: No; and the compiler warns about it
optionC: No; zero is the only value that counts as false
optionD: It depends on whether the zero is written or computed
correctAnswerText: No; zero is the only value that counts as false
explanation: Zero is false and everything else is true, whether the zero was written down or produced by a calculation. Nothing warns about it, which is why a computed zero can quietly disable a branch.

prompt: A C fragment reads: int x = 7; if (x > 5) printf("A"); else printf("B"); What is printed?
optionA: B
optionB: A
optionD: Nothing, since the condition is not stored anywhere
correctAnswerText: A
explanation: The comparison produces a non-zero value, so the first branch runs and the second is skipped. A condition does not need to be stored to be acted on.

prompt: Which C loop form always executes its body at least once?
optionA: while
optionB: for
optionC: None of them; every loop tests before running
optionD: do ... while
correctAnswerText: do ... while
explanation: The do form tests after the body, so the body has already run by the time the condition is examined. Both other forms test first and may run zero times.

prompt: A C while loop is reached with its condition already false. How many times does the body run?
optionA: None
optionB: Once, and then the condition is checked
optionC: Once, because a loop always runs its body
optionD: It does not compile
correctAnswerText: None
explanation: A while loop checks before it runs, so a condition false at entry means the body is skipped entirely. Running once regardless is what the do form would do.

prompt: A menu must be shown and then repeated until the user chooses to quit. Which loop form fits most naturally?
optionA: while, because the choice must be tested first
optionB: for, because the number of repetitions is known
optionC: do ... while, because the menu should appear before any choice exists to test
optionD: Any of them; the forms are interchangeable
correctAnswerText: do ... while, because the menu should appear before any choice exists to test
explanation: There is nothing to test until the menu has been shown once, which is exactly the situation the test-after form exists for. A test-first loop would need a value invented before the first display.

prompt: A while loop and a do ... while loop have identical bodies and identical conditions. On what input do they behave differently?
optionA: Input for which the condition never becomes false
optionB: Input for which the condition is false at entry: one runs the body zero times and the other once
optionC: Input for which the body runs many times
optionD: They never behave differently
correctAnswerText: Input for which the condition is false at entry: one runs the body zero times and the other once
explanation: Once the body has run at all, the two forms proceed identically. Their only difference is what happens before the first test, which is visible only when the condition starts out false.

prompt: A C fragment reads: int x = 0; if (x = 5) printf("A"); What happens, and what does x hold afterwards?
optionA: Nothing is printed, and x holds 0
optionB: Nothing is printed, and x holds 5
optionC: The fragment does not compile
optionD: A is printed, and x holds 5
correctAnswerText: A is printed, and x holds 5
explanation: A single equals assigns and then yields the value assigned, which is non-zero and so satisfies the condition. Both effects happen, which is why answering only one of them misses half of what the line does.

prompt: A loop is written as: int n = 3; while (n = 0) { n--; } How many times does the body run, and what does n hold at the end?
optionA: Zero times, and n holds 0
optionB: Three times, and n holds 0
optionC: Zero times, and n holds 3
optionD: Endlessly, because n is set to 0 every time round
correctAnswerText: Zero times, and n holds 0
explanation: The assignment stores 0 in n and yields 0, which is false, so the loop never enters its body. The variable is changed all the same — a comparison would have run the body three times, which is what a single equals silently costs here.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (a > 0) if (b > 0) printf("X"); else printf("Y"); with the else indented to line up with the first if. Which if does the else belong to?
optionA: The outer one, on a, as the indentation shows
optionB: Both, since neither has braces
optionC: The inner one, on b
optionD: Neither; the fragment does not compile
correctAnswerText: The inner one, on b
explanation: An else attaches to the nearest unmatched if, and indentation has no bearing on it. Lining the else up with the outer if makes the code read as something it is not.

prompt: The same fragment runs with a = -1 and b = 5. What is printed?
optionA: Y, because a is not positive
optionB: Nothing
optionC: X, because b is positive
optionD: Both X and Y
correctAnswerText: Nothing
explanation: The outer condition fails, so everything inside it is skipped — including the else, which belongs to the inner if. A reader who binds the else to the outer if expects Y, which is exactly what the misleading indentation invites.

prompt: A C fragment reads: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) printf("%d ", i); What is printed?
explanation: The counter starts at 0 and the loop stops before 3, so 0 1 2 appears. Reading the condition as inclusive adds a fourth value that never occurs.

prompt: How many times does the body run in: for (int i = 2; i <= 11; i += 3)?
explanation: The counter takes 2, 5, 8 and 11, and the last of those satisfies the inclusive condition, so the body runs 4 times. With a step other than one the count is not the difference between the bounds, which is where 9 comes from.

prompt: A C fragment reads: for (int i = 10; i > 0; i++) and the program never finishes. The condition and the starting value are both sensible on their own. What is wrong?
optionA: The starting value should be 0
optionB: The condition should be i >= 0
optionC: The step moves away from the bound, so the condition can never become false
optionD: A for loop cannot count downwards
correctAnswerText: The step moves away from the bound, so the condition can never become false
explanation: A counted loop only ends if its step drives the counter toward the bound, and here it drives it away. Both the start and the condition are perfectly reasonable — it is the relationship between the three parts that fails.

prompt: A counter declared outside a loop runs: for (i = 0; i < 4; i++). What does i hold immediately after the loop?
explanation: The loop ends when the condition first fails, which happens once i has reached 4. The last value used inside the body was 3, which is one less.

prompt: A counter declared outside a loop runs: for (i = 1; i <= 6; i += 2). What does i hold immediately after the loop?
explanation: The counter takes 1, 3 and 5 inside the body, and the step then makes it 7, which fails the condition. The bound itself is never reached, because the step passes over it.

prompt: A program uses the counter after the loop to report how many items were processed, and the figure is always one too high. Each item was processed exactly once. What is wrong?
optionA: The counter holds the value that failed the condition, which is one past the last item
optionB: The loop processes one item too many
optionC: The counter should have started at 1
optionD: The counter is being incremented twice per pass
correctAnswerText: The counter holds the value that failed the condition, which is one past the last item
explanation: Every item being processed once rules out an extra pass, so the count is wrong rather than the work. The counter necessarily ends one beyond the last value it used, which is exactly the discrepancy reported.

prompt: A C fragment declares int sum; without assigning it, then adds three values to it in a loop. What does sum hold at the end?
optionA: The sum of the three values
optionB: Zero, because sum was declared
optionC: The three values added to whatever was already in that memory
optionD: Nothing; the program does not compile
correctAnswerText: The three values added to whatever was already in that memory
explanation: Declaring reserves space without clearing it, so the loop adds to rubbish. The program compiles and runs, which is what makes the wrong total so hard to account for.

prompt: A C function sets a running total to zero, then adds each whole number from 1 to 3 inclusive to it, then reports the total. What does it report?
explanation: The values 1, 2 and 3 accumulate to 6. Answering 3 reports the last value added rather than the accumulated result, and 0 reports the starting value.

prompt: A C program sums an array and prints a plausible but wrong total, and prints a different wrong total each time it runs. The array and the loop bounds are correct. What is wrong?
optionA: The total is being initialised inside the loop
optionB: The array is being read one item past its end
optionC: The total is declared with too small a type
optionD: The running total was never initialised, so each run starts from whatever was in that memory
correctAnswerText: The running total was never initialised, so each run starts from whatever was in that memory
explanation: A different answer on each run is the signature of an unset starting value, since the code and the data are identical between runs. Initialising inside the loop would give the same wrong answer every time.

prompt: A break is reached inside the inner of two nested C loops. Where does execution continue?
optionA: Immediately after the inner loop, still inside the outer one
optionB: Immediately after the outer loop
optionC: At the next iteration of the inner loop
optionD: At the start of the outer loop
correctAnswerText: Immediately after the inner loop, still inside the outer one
explanation: A break leaves exactly one enclosing structure, which is the innermost. Skipping one iteration is what a different instruction does, and leaving both loops needs something more than a plain break.

prompt: A search examines each row of a table, and within each row it abandons the row as soon as its second entry has been checked. The table has 3 rows of 4 entries. How many entries are checked?
explanation: Two entries are checked in each row, because the pass that abandons the row has already examined that entry, and all 3 rows are still visited — 6 entries in all. Abandoning a row ends only the inner structure, so the outer traversal continues.

prompt: A search over a two-dimensional array is meant to stop entirely once a value is found, and it keeps searching later rows. The break is present and does execute. What is wrong?
optionA: The break is inside a conditional and never runs
optionB: The break leaves only the inner loop, so the outer loop begins the next row
optionC: The comparison never matches, so the break is not reached
optionD: The break should have been placed after the inner loop
correctAnswerText: The break leaves only the inner loop, so the outer loop begins the next row
explanation: The break executing rules out it being unreached, and later rows still being searched shows only one structure was left. Stopping both needs a flag the outer loop tests, or a return.

prompt: A multi-way selection on a value has a case for 1 and a case for 2, each ending with a break, and no default. The value is 2. Which cases run?
optionA: Only the case for 1
optionB: Both cases, in the order written
optionC: None, because no default is present
optionD: Only the case for 2
correctAnswerText: Only the case for 2
explanation: Execution enters at the matching case, and the break there leaves the structure before any other case is reached. A missing default is not an error; it means only that an unmatched value would do nothing.

prompt: A multi-way selection is written with three cases and the first of them has no break: int x = 1; switch (x) { case 1: printf("A"); case 2: printf("B"); break; case 3: printf("C"); break; } What appears?
optionA: A then B
optionB: A
optionC: A, B then C
optionD: B
correctAnswerText: A then B
explanation: Execution enters at the matching case and continues until a break, so the missing break after the first case lets the second run too. It stops at the break before the third.

prompt: A multi-way selection is meant to handle three values separately, and two of them produce the output of the next case as well. The third behaves correctly. What is wrong?
optionA: The values being matched are wrong
optionB: The default case is missing
optionC: The first two cases have no break, so execution continues into the following case
optionD: The cases are written in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: The first two cases have no break, so execution continues into the following case
explanation: One case behaving correctly shows the structure and the matching work, and the other two producing extra output is exactly what falling through the end of a case does. Order does not affect which case is entered.

prompt: A nested C pair prints i then j on each inner pass: for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) for (j = 0; j < 2; j++) printf("%d%d ", i, j); What is printed?
explanation: The inner loop runs fully for each value of i, so the pairs come out in the order 00 01 10 11. Answering 00 11 advances both counters together, which is what treating the pair as a single loop would do.

prompt: An inner counter is declared outside both loops and is not reset at the start of each outer pass. The outer loop runs 3 times and the inner condition is j < 4. The inner body runs 4 times in total rather than 12. Why?
optionA: The outer loop ran only once
optionB: The inner loop breaks on its fourth pass
optionC: The inner bound should have been 12
optionD: The counter kept its value from the first pass, so the inner condition was already false afterwards
correctAnswerText: The counter kept its value from the first pass, so the inner condition was already false afterwards
explanation: A counter left at 4 fails the condition immediately on every later outer pass, so the inner body never runs again. Declaring the counter inside the loop, or resetting it, is what makes the counts multiply.

prompt: A C function loops over an array and contains a return inside the loop body, not inside any conditional. How many items does it examine?
optionA: One; the return ends the function on the first pass
optionB: All of them; the loop finishes first
optionC: All of them; a return inside a loop acts as a break
optionD: None; the return is reached before the loop begins
correctAnswerText: One; the return ends the function on the first pass
explanation: A return leaves the function immediately, so nothing after it runs and no later pass happens. It is stronger than a break, which leaves only the loop.

prompt: A C function is meant to return the largest value in an array. It returns the first value every time. The comparison inside the loop is correct and the loop bounds are correct. What is wrong?
optionA: The comparison is the wrong way round
optionB: The running maximum starts at zero
optionC: The return sits inside the loop body rather than after it
optionD: The loop examines only the first item because of its bounds
correctAnswerText: The return sits inside the loop body rather than after it
explanation: Correct bounds and a correct comparison leave only where the value is handed back. Returning on the first pass gives the first value whatever the rest of the array holds, which is exactly the symptom.

prompt: A C loop is written as: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++); { printf("%d", i); } It compiles, runs, and prints nothing about the loop. What is wrong?
optionA: The loop condition is never true
optionB: The semicolon ends the loop body, so the braced block runs once, outside the loop
optionC: The braces are not allowed after a for statement
optionD: The printf uses the wrong specifier
correctAnswerText: The semicolon ends the loop body, so the braced block runs once, outside the loop
explanation: The loop repeats an empty statement five times and then the block runs once on its own. It is entirely legal, which is why nothing is reported.

prompt: A C loop is meant to run a two-statement body and only the first statement repeats. It compiles cleanly and the two statements are indented identically. What is wrong?
optionA: A semicolon after the condition ended the body
optionB: The second statement is placed before the loop
optionC: The loop condition becomes false after one pass
optionD: There are no braces, so the loop governs only the first statement
correctAnswerText: There are no braces, so the loop governs only the first statement
explanation: Only the first statement repeating points at what the loop governs, and without braces that is exactly one statement. A semicolon after the condition would have made neither statement repeat.

prompt: Three C faults are all silent: a semicolon after a loop condition, missing braces around a two-statement body, and an else bound to the wrong if. What do they have in common, and why is that dangerous?
optionA: Each produces a valid program with a different meaning, so the compiler has nothing to report and the code reads as intended
optionB: Each produces a compiler warning that is easy to ignore
optionC: Each causes the program to stop at run time
optionD: Each is caught by testing the ordinary cases
correctAnswerText: Each produces a valid program with a different meaning, so the compiler has nothing to report and the code reads as intended
explanation: All three are legal C that means something other than what the layout suggests, which is why nothing complains and why reading the code does not reveal them. Testing may not catch them either, since the ordinary case can happen to give the right answer.

prompt: A team adopts a rule that braces are always written, even around a single statement. What does that prevent, and what does it cost?
optionA: It prevents the semicolon fault, and costs nothing
optionB: It prevents nothing, since a single statement needs no braces
optionC: It prevents a later added line from silently falling outside the structure; it costs two lines of text per conditional
optionD: It costs performance, since braces create a block
correctAnswerText: It prevents a later added line from silently falling outside the structure; it costs two lines of text per conditional
explanation: The danger is not the code as first written but the line somebody adds to it later, which joins the block if braces are there and does not if they are not. Braces are free at run time; the cost is purely in text.

prompt: A C program behaves correctly on every test and contains a missing pair of braces around a two-statement conditional body. How can both be true?
optionA: The compiler inserted the braces automatically
optionB: The tests never exercised a case where the second statement should have been skipped
optionC: Missing braces have no effect when the body is short
optionD: The tests are wrong, since the program cannot be correct
correctAnswerText: The tests never exercised a case where the second statement should have been skipped
explanation: The second statement runs unconditionally, which is only visible on input where the condition is false. If every test satisfies the condition, the fault and the correct code behave identically.

prompt: A C fragment declares int total; then runs a for loop whose condition is false at entry, then prints total. It prints a large unrelated number. The loop body is correct. What happened?
optionA: The loop ran once before the condition was checked
optionB: The loop ran and the body produced a wrong total
optionC: The program printed the loop counter rather than the total
optionD: The loop ran zero times, so total kept the rubbish it was declared with
correctAnswerText: The loop ran zero times, so total kept the rubbish it was declared with
explanation: Two facts combine: a test-first loop can run zero times, and a declared variable holds rubbish until assigned. Either alone would be harmless, and together they print a plausible-looking number that came from nowhere.

prompt: A do ... while loop is given input for which its condition is false from the very start. What does it produce?
optionA: One pass of the body, since the condition is tested only afterwards
optionB: No passes, like a while loop
optionC: An error, since the condition was never true
optionD: Endless passes, since the condition was never true
correctAnswerText: One pass of the body, since the condition is tested only afterwards
explanation: The test-after form has already run its body by the time the condition is examined. That single guaranteed pass is the whole difference between the two forms, and it appears only at this boundary.

prompt: A loop summing an array is given an array of size zero. The total was initialised to 0 before the loop. What is printed?
optionA: An unpredictable value, since the loop never ran
optionB: An error, since an array cannot have size zero
optionC: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
optionD: The value of the loop counter
correctAnswerText: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
explanation: The loop runs zero times and the total keeps the value it was given, which is the right answer for summing nothing. The initialisation is what makes the empty case safe — without it the same loop would print rubbish.

prompt: A loop is meant to run a number of times read from input. What should be checked before it runs, and which loop form makes the check more urgent?
optionA: That the count is not zero; the test-first form, which would loop endlessly
optionB: That the count is not zero or negative; the test-after form, which runs once regardless
optionC: Nothing; a loop handles any count correctly
optionD: That the count is not too large; either form is equally affected
correctAnswerText: That the count is not zero or negative; the test-after form, which runs once regardless
explanation: A test-first loop handles a count of zero correctly by running nothing, so it needs no guard for that case. A test-after loop runs once whatever the count says, which is wrong for zero and worse for a negative value.

prompt: Two C loops differ only in that one initialises its accumulator and one does not. On ordinary input they agree. Where do they part company?
optionA: On large input, where the uninitialised one overflows
optionB: On negative input, where the uninitialised one wraps
optionC: Nowhere; the first pass assigns the accumulator either way
optionD: On input that makes the loop run zero times, where one prints its starting value and the other prints rubbish
correctAnswerText: On input that makes the loop run zero times, where one prints its starting value and the other prints rubbish
explanation: Once the loop runs at least once and the accumulator is assigned before being read, the two behave identically — which is why ordinary testing finds nothing. Only zero iterations leave the starting value visible.

prompt: A while loop is rewritten as a do ... while loop with the same body and condition. They agree on every input the program has been given. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they differ on input for which the condition is false at entry
optionB: Yes; the two forms are interchangeable
optionC: No; they differ whenever the loop runs more than once
optionD: No; they differ on input for which the loop never ends
correctAnswerText: No; they differ on input for which the condition is false at entry
explanation: Every input tested happened to satisfy the condition at least once, which is where the two forms agree. The separating case is the one the testing never produced.

prompt: A chain of else-if branches is rewritten as three separate if statements with the same conditions and bodies. Are the two equivalent?
optionA: Yes; the same conditions select the same branches
optionB: No; separate statements cannot use the same conditions
optionC: No; where two conditions both hold, the chain runs one branch and the separate statements run both
optionD: Yes, provided the conditions are written in the same order
correctAnswerText: No; where two conditions both hold, the chain runs one branch and the separate statements run both
explanation: A chain stops at its first true condition and separate statements each test independently, so the two agree exactly when no two conditions can hold together. With disjoint conditions they are genuinely equivalent, which is what makes this worth checking rather than assuming.

prompt: A for loop is rewritten as a while loop with the initialisation before it and the step at the end of the body. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes, in every case
optionB: Yes for an ordinary body, but not if the body contains a continue, which skips the step in the while version
optionC: No; a for loop can never be written as a while loop
optionD: No; the counter is scoped differently, which changes the result
correctAnswerText: Yes for an ordinary body, but not if the body contains a continue, which skips the step in the while version
explanation: The two forms run the same three parts in the same order until something jumps to the next pass. A continue in the for version still performs the step, and in the rewritten version it skips it, which turns a terminating loop into an endless one.

prompt: Two fragments are equivalent for every input. One uses a multi-way selection and one uses a chain of conditionals. On what grounds should the choice be made?
optionA: On the multi-way selection, which is always faster
optionB: On the chain, which is always clearer
optionC: On neither; equivalent fragments are interchangeable in every respect
optionD: On which states the intent more directly, since behaviour no longer separates them
correctAnswerText: On which states the intent more directly, since behaviour no longer separates them
explanation: Equivalence settles correctness and leaves everything else open, so what remains is whether the next reader can see the structure of the decision. Neither form is universally clearer — a multi-way selection suits matching one value, a chain suits ranges.

prompt: Which of these jobs is done by the processor?
optionA: Keeping files so they survive a restart
optionB: Carrying out the instructions a program contains
optionC: Deciding which program is allowed to run next
optionD: Holding the pictures shown on the screen
correctAnswerText: Carrying out the instructions a program contains
explanation: The processor executes instructions; that is what it is for. Keeping files is storage, deciding what runs next is the operating system's decision, and holding an image is memory.

prompt: Is the processor where a computer's files are kept?
optionA: Yes; the processor holds everything the machine has
optionB: Yes, but only the files currently open
optionC: No; files are kept in the operating system
optionD: No; files are kept on storage, and the processor holds almost nothing
correctAnswerText: No; files are kept on storage, and the processor holds almost nothing
explanation: The processor works on values handed to it and keeps only a few at a time. Confusing it with storage makes the rest of the machine's arrangement impossible to explain.

prompt: Is the processor hardware or software?
optionA: Hardware; it is a physical component
optionB: Software; it is a set of instructions
optionC: Software; it is part of the operating system
optionD: Neither; it is a way of describing what a machine does
correctAnswerText: Hardware; it is a physical component
explanation: The processor is a physical part that instructions are given to. Instructions are what run on it, which is exactly the distinction the question turns on.

prompt: A machine displays an image on screen. Which part of that is the processor's job?
optionA: Holding the image while it is displayed
optionB: Turning the values into light on the panel
optionC: Working out the values that describe the image
optionD: Deciding which application may use the screen
correctAnswerText: Working out the values that describe the image
explanation: The processor computes; other parts hold the result, display it, and arbitrate access to it. Attributing everything the machine does to the processor is the error being probed.

prompt: Which component mainly executes program instructions?
optionA: Working memory
optionB: The processor
optionC: The storage drive
optionD: The keyboard
correctAnswerText: The processor
explanation: Instructions are fetched from memory and carried out by the processor. Memory holds them and storage keeps them between runs; neither performs them.

prompt: Two numbers are added together. Which unit performs the addition?
optionA: The control unit
optionB: Working memory
optionC: The operating system
optionD: The arithmetic and logic unit
correctAnswerText: The arithmetic and logic unit
explanation: The arithmetic and logic unit is the part built to carry arithmetic out. The control unit decides what happens next, memory holds the values, and the operating system issues no arithmetic of its own here.

prompt: Two values are compared to see which is larger. Which unit performs the comparison?
optionA: The arithmetic and logic unit, which handles logic as well as arithmetic
optionB: The control unit, since a comparison controls what happens next
optionC: Working memory, where the two values are held
optionD: The operating system, which decides the outcome
correctAnswerText: The arithmetic and logic unit, which handles logic as well as arithmetic
explanation: The unit's name covers logic as well as arithmetic, and a comparison is a logic operation. That its result then influences what runs next is a separate step performed by the control unit.

prompt: What does the control unit do?
optionA: Performs the calculations the instructions ask for
optionB: Holds the program while it runs
optionC: Works out what each instruction means and directs the other parts accordingly
optionD: Stores the results of each instruction
correctAnswerText: Works out what each instruction means and directs the other parts accordingly
explanation: The control unit interprets and directs; it produces no values of its own. Reading "control" as "does the work" is exactly the misreading the name invites.

prompt: An instruction says to multiply two values. Which part decides that a multiplication is what is wanted, and which part produces the answer?
optionA: The arithmetic and logic unit decides and produces the answer
optionB: The control unit decides; the arithmetic and logic unit produces the answer
optionC: The control unit decides and produces the answer
optionD: Working memory decides; the control unit produces the answer
correctAnswerText: The control unit decides; the arithmetic and logic unit produces the answer
explanation: Interpreting the instruction and performing it are two jobs done by two parts. Assigning both to one of them collapses the distinction the two units exist to make.

prompt: What do registers hold?
optionA: The whole of the program currently running
optionB: Files that must survive a restart
optionC: A copy of everything in working memory
