optionD: The few values the processor is working with at this moment
correctAnswerText: The few values the processor is working with at this moment
explanation: Registers hold a very small number of values, right where the work happens. Anything larger lives further out, in memory or on storage.

prompt: How do registers compare with working memory?
optionA: Far faster and far smaller
optionB: Faster and larger
optionC: Slower and smaller
optionD: The same speed, and simply nearer
correctAnswerText: Far faster and far smaller
explanation: Speed and capacity run in opposite directions across the whole arrangement, and registers sit at the fast, tiny end of it. Being both faster and larger would remove the reason for having memory at all.

prompt: What happens to the contents of working memory when a machine is switched off?
optionA: They are kept until the machine is switched on again
optionB: They are written to storage automatically
optionC: They are lost
optionD: They are kept for a few hours and then lost
correctAnswerText: They are lost
explanation: Working memory holds what is needed while the machine runs and keeps nothing without power. That is precisely why saving a file writes it somewhere else.

prompt: Which of these is kept in working memory while a program runs?
optionA: The program's files, permanently
optionB: The values the program is currently using
optionC: The operating system's installation, permanently
optionD: Nothing; a running program uses only the processor
correctAnswerText: The values the program is currently using
explanation: Working memory holds what is in use now, and gives it up when the program ends. Permanent copies of anything live on storage.

prompt: Does adding more working memory make the processor faster?
optionA: Yes; more memory means faster calculation
optionB: Yes; the processor runs at the speed of the memory
optionC: No; adding memory has no effect on anything
optionD: No; it lets more be held at once, which is a different thing
correctAnswerText: No; it lets more be held at once, which is a different thing
explanation: More memory removes the need to shuffle data to and from storage, which can make a machine feel much faster without the processor doing anything more quickly. The two are separate quantities.

prompt: A machine has plenty of storage and very little working memory. What is the likely effect?
optionA: Programs run, but the machine spends much of its time moving data between memory and storage
optionB: Programs cannot be installed at all
optionC: Programs run at full speed, since storage makes up the difference
optionD: The processor runs more slowly to compensate
correctAnswerText: Programs run, but the machine spends much of its time moving data between memory and storage
explanation: Storage can stand in for memory and is far slower, so the work still happens and takes much longer. Installation depends on storage, which the machine has.

prompt: A value must still be available after the machine has been switched off and on again. Where should it be kept?
optionA: In working memory
optionB: In a processor register
optionC: On storage
optionD: In the processor cache
correctAnswerText: On storage
explanation: Only storage keeps its contents without power. Each of the other three is faster and loses everything when the machine stops.

prompt: A value is read millions of times while a program runs and does not need to survive the program ending. Where is it best kept?
optionA: On storage, so that it is safe
optionB: In working memory, or nearer the processor still
optionC: On storage, since it is read so often
optionD: Nowhere; a value read that often should be recomputed each time
correctAnswerText: In working memory, or nearer the processor still
explanation: The requirement is speed and not survival, which points inward rather than outward. Keeping it on storage would make every one of those millions of reads far slower for a guarantee nobody asked for.

prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest: working memory, a processor register, a storage drive.
optionA: Working memory, register, storage drive
optionB: Storage drive, working memory, register
optionC: Register, storage drive, working memory
optionD: Register, working memory, storage drive
correctAnswerText: Register, working memory, storage drive
explanation: Speed increases with nearness to the processor, so registers lead and storage trails. The ordering by capacity runs the other way.

prompt: Order the same three from largest capacity to smallest.
optionA: Storage drive, working memory, register
optionB: Register, working memory, storage drive
optionC: Working memory, storage drive, register
optionD: They are all about the same size
correctAnswerText: Storage drive, working memory, register
explanation: Capacity runs opposite to speed, so the slowest layer is the largest. Getting both orders the same way round is the answer that shows the trade-off has not landed.

prompt: Someone proposes building a machine whose memory is as fast as a register and as large as a storage drive. Every layer of the existing arrangement exists because no such thing is available. What is wrong with the proposal?
optionA: Nothing; such memory already exists and is simply not used
optionB: Registers cannot be made larger under any circumstances
optionC: Nothing is wrong with wanting it; the arrangement exists precisely because speed and capacity cannot both be maximised affordably
optionD: A single layer would be slower than several
correctAnswerText: Nothing is wrong with wanting it; the arrangement exists precisely because speed and capacity cannot both be maximised affordably
explanation: The proposal describes exactly what would make the hierarchy unnecessary, which is why the hierarchy exists. The obstacle is cost and physics rather than an oversight in how machines are built.

prompt: A machine's cache is described as being larger than its working memory. Every other layer in the machine follows the usual arrangement. Why is that description suspect?
optionA: Cache and memory are the same thing under two names
optionB: Cache sits nearer the processor than memory, so it is faster and correspondingly smaller
optionC: Cache is always exactly half the size of memory
optionD: Nothing is suspect; cache size varies freely
correctAnswerText: Cache sits nearer the processor than memory, so it is faster and correspondingly smaller
explanation: Each layer trades capacity for speed against the one beyond it, and cache is on the fast side of memory. A layer that was both faster and larger would make the layer beyond it pointless.

prompt: Which pair contains one input device and one output device?
optionA: Monitor and speaker
optionB: Mouse and scanner
optionC: Printer and speaker
optionD: Keyboard and monitor
correctAnswerText: Keyboard and monitor
explanation: A keyboard brings data in and a monitor sends it out. Each of the other pairs has both devices travelling in the same direction.

prompt: A touchscreen displays images and registers where it is touched. How should it be classified?
optionA: Both input and output
optionB: Output only, because it is a screen
optionC: Input only, because it is touched
optionD: Neither, because it does both
correctAnswerText: Both input and output
explanation: Classification follows what the data does, and here it travels in both directions. Deciding from the device category rather than from the data is what makes a screen look like output only.

prompt: A storage drive has data written to it and read from it. How should it be classified?
optionA: Neither; storage is a separate category
optionB: Output only, since data is written to it
optionC: Both input and output
optionD: Input only, since data is read from it
correctAnswerText: Both input and output
explanation: Data travels into the drive and back out of it, so both directions occur. Treating storage as a category outside the classification is the answer that avoids applying the rule at all.

prompt: What does a bus do?
optionA: Stores data on the way between components
optionB: Carries signals between components along a shared route
optionC: Connects exactly two components to each other
optionD: Converts data from one form to another
correctAnswerText: Carries signals between components along a shared route
explanation: A bus is a route rather than a place, and several components share it. Storing anything is the job of memory, and a shared route is what makes a bus different from a direct connection.

prompt: A value is read from memory into the processor. Besides the value itself, what else must travel?
optionA: Nothing else; the value alone is enough
optionB: The whole of the surrounding memory, from which the value is picked
optionC: The instruction that asked for the value
optionD: Which location is wanted, and a signal saying that a read is what is being asked for
correctAnswerText: Which location is wanted, and a signal saying that a read is what is being asked for
explanation: Memory has to be told where to look and what to do, so an address and a control signal accompany the data. Believing only data travels is the half-formed model this measures.

prompt: Put the stages of handling one instruction in order.
optionA: Fetch, decode, execute
optionB: Decode, fetch, execute
optionC: Fetch, execute, decode
optionD: Execute, fetch, decode
correctAnswerText: Fetch, decode, execute
explanation: An instruction has to be collected before it can be interpreted, and interpreted before it can be carried out. Decoding first would require understanding something not yet obtained.

prompt: How many times does that sequence of stages run while a program of a thousand instructions executes?
optionA: Once, covering the whole program
optionB: Three times, once per stage
optionC: About a thousand times, once for each instruction
optionD: Once per line of source code the programmer wrote
correctAnswerText: About a thousand times, once for each instruction
explanation: The cycle handles a single instruction and repeats for the next, which is what makes a processor able to run a program of any length. Treating it as covering the whole program misses the repetition entirely.

prompt: An instruction adds a value held in memory to one already in the processor. Where does the memory value go first?
optionA: Straight into the arithmetic and logic unit from memory
optionB: Into a register inside the processor
optionC: Onto storage, and then into the processor
optionD: Into the control unit, which performs the addition
correctAnswerText: Into a register inside the processor
explanation: Values are brought into registers before they are operated on, which is what registers are for. The arithmetic unit works on what the registers hold rather than reaching into memory itself.

prompt: A result has just been computed. Someone says it is written directly to the storage drive. The program did not ask for anything to be saved. Where does it actually go?
optionA: To the storage drive, as they said
optionB: Back into the control unit for checking
optionC: Nowhere; it is used and discarded within the arithmetic unit
optionD: Into a register, and then to memory if the program keeps it
correctAnswerText: Into a register, and then to memory if the program keeps it
explanation: Reaching storage requires an explicit request, and none was made. A computed value lands in a register and travels no further unless the program stores it.

prompt: A single instruction is traced and the value appears never to enter a register at all, going straight from memory to the arithmetic unit. Every other instruction in the trace does use a register. What is the likely explanation?
optionA: The trace has omitted the step; the register is where operands are held for the arithmetic unit
optionB: This instruction is a special kind that bypasses registers
optionC: The arithmetic unit contains its own memory for such cases
optionD: The value was small enough not to need a register
correctAnswerText: The trace has omitted the step; the register is where operands are held for the arithmetic unit
explanation: One instruction behaving unlike every other in the same trace points at the record rather than at the machine. Operands reach the arithmetic unit through registers, and the size of a value does not change that.

prompt: Trace where a value is at each point while one instruction adds it to another: it begins on the storage drive and the program has just started. What is the full path?
optionA: Storage to the arithmetic unit, result to memory
optionB: Storage to a register, register to memory, memory to the arithmetic unit
optionC: Storage to memory, memory to a register, register to the arithmetic unit, result back to a register
optionD: Memory to the arithmetic unit, result to storage
correctAnswerText: Storage to memory, memory to a register, register to the arithmetic unit, result back to a register
explanation: Each layer hands on to the next one inward, and the result comes back out the way it went in. Skipping memory or reaching the arithmetic unit from storage removes a step the machine cannot do without.

prompt: A value is used repeatedly by a tight piece of code. Where would you expect it to be after the first few uses, and why?
optionA: Written back to storage after each use, for safety
optionB: In a register or cache, because the machine keeps recently used values near the processor
optionC: In working memory, since that is where all values live
optionD: Recomputed each time, since holding it costs space
correctAnswerText: In a register or cache, because the machine keeps recently used values near the processor
explanation: Repeated use is exactly the condition the inner layers exist for, so a value read again and again is kept close. Writing it out after each use would pay the largest cost available on every use.

prompt: Which digit values are used in binary?
optionA: 0 to 9
optionB: 1 and 2
optionC: A and B
optionD: 0 and 1
correctAnswerText: 0 and 1
explanation: Binary uses exactly two digit values. Everything a machine holds — numbers, text, images, sound — is built from them.

prompt: The same pattern of bits is opened as a number by one program and as text by another, and each shows something different. How is that possible?
optionA: The bits carry no meaning of their own; what they represent is decided by how they are interpreted
optionB: One of the two programs has misread the bits
optionC: The bits change depending on which program opens them
optionD: Text and numbers are stored in different ways, so one of the two is wrong
correctAnswerText: The bits carry no meaning of their own; what they represent is decided by how they are interpreted
explanation: Storage holds patterns and nothing else, and meaning is supplied by whatever reads them. This is why opening a file with the wrong program shows nonsense rather than reporting an error.

prompt: A machine copying large files between drives shows the processor almost idle throughout. Which component limits the work?
optionA: The processor
optionB: Working memory
optionC: The drives
optionD: The display
correctAnswerText: The drives
explanation: An idle processor cannot be what is holding the work up. Copying moves data between drives and is limited by how fast they can read and write it.

prompt: A task takes far longer than expected. The processor sits near idle, the drives are busy continuously, and there is ample free memory. Someone proposes a faster processor. Would it help?
optionA: Yes; a faster processor speeds up every task
optionB: No; the processor is not what the work is waiting on, so a faster one would sit idle just as often
optionC: Yes; the drives would be driven harder by a faster processor
optionD: No; more memory is what is needed
correctAnswerText: No; the processor is not what the work is waiting on, so a faster one would sit idle just as often
explanation: The evidence names the busy component and the idle one, which settles where the limit is. Adding memory would not help either, since the stem says there is already plenty.

prompt: A calculation runs slowly. The processor is fully used, the drives are quiet and memory is largely free. Which change would help most?
optionA: A larger storage drive
optionB: More working memory
optionC: A faster network connection
optionD: A faster processor, or spreading the work across more of them
correctAnswerText: A faster processor, or spreading the work across more of them
explanation: The fully used component is the one holding the work up, and here it is the processor. Each other change addresses a resource the evidence shows is not under pressure.

prompt: A machine is upgraded with a much faster processor and the task it was bought for runs barely faster. What does that tell you, and what should be measured next?
optionA: The processor was not the limit; measure which component is busy while the task runs
optionB: The upgrade was faulty and should be replaced
optionC: The task cannot be made faster by any hardware
optionD: The processor must be faster still
correctAnswerText: The processor was not the limit; measure which component is busy while the task runs
explanation: An upgrade that changes nothing is evidence about where the limit is not, which narrows the search rather than exhausting it. Buying a faster version of the same component again is what the observation argues against.

prompt: After a component is upgraded and the task speeds up, the same task is now limited by a different component. Is that a sign the upgrade was wrong?
optionA: Yes; a correct upgrade removes the limit entirely
optionB: Yes; the new limit shows the wrong component was chosen
optionC: No; relieving one limit always exposes the next one, and the task did get faster
optionD: No, but the second limit means the first was not a limit at all
correctAnswerText: No; relieving one limit always exposes the next one, and the task did get faster
explanation: Something is always the slowest part, so removing one bottleneck necessarily reveals another. Whether the upgrade was worth it is settled by how much faster the task became, not by whether a limit remains.

prompt: Two upgrades are affordable and only one can be bought. One removes a limit that costs the task ten minutes a day; the other removes a limit costing two minutes a day and is cheaper. How should the choice be made?
optionA: Always the larger saving, since time matters most
optionB: By comparing what each buys against what each costs, since the larger saving is not automatically the better purchase
optionC: Always the cheaper one, since budgets are limited
optionD: Neither; both limits should be removed together
correctAnswerText: By comparing what each buys against what each costs, since the larger saving is not automatically the better purchase
explanation: Two quantities are in play and neither dominates by itself, so the decision needs both. A rule that looks only at the saving, or only at the price, is a preference standing in for a calculation.

prompt: A machine is needed to hold a very large archive that is read rarely, and the budget is tight. Speed is explicitly not a priority. Which configuration is defensible?
optionA: The fastest drive available, at whatever capacity fits the budget
optionB: A large amount of working memory instead of storage
optionC: A configuration that is fastest, largest and cheapest at once
optionD: A large, slower drive, accepting that reads take longer
correctAnswerText: A large, slower drive, accepting that reads take longer
explanation: The stated priorities are capacity and cost, and the answer gives up the thing that was said not to matter. The last option claims to win on every axis, which is what the trade-off says is unavailable.

prompt: A machine must serve a small dataset to many users as quickly as possible, and capacity is not a concern. The whole dataset fits comfortably in memory. Which configuration is defensible?
optionA: Enough memory to hold the dataset, and a fast processor, with modest storage
optionB: The largest storage drive available
optionC: Minimal memory, with the dataset read from storage each time
optionD: A configuration chosen for lowest cost across every component
correctAnswerText: Enough memory to hold the dataset, and a fast processor, with modest storage
explanation: The stated priority is speed for a small dataset, and the stem confirms it fits in memory, which removes the reason to buy capacity. Reading from storage each time gives up exactly what was asked for.

prompt: A supplier claims a configuration that is faster, larger and cheaper than every alternative. What is the first thing to check?
optionA: Nothing; a better configuration is simply better
optionB: Whether the price includes delivery
optionC: What it gives up that the comparison did not measure — durability, reliability, or how the figures were obtained
optionD: Whether the components are from the same manufacturer
correctAnswerText: What it gives up that the comparison did not measure — durability, reliability, or how the figures were obtained
explanation: Winning on every axis at once is what the trade-off says does not happen, so the claim points at an axis nobody compared. That is a reason to look harder rather than to reject it outright.

prompt: A budget can buy either much more memory or a much faster processor. The workload is not yet known. What follows?
optionA: Buy the processor, since it affects everything
optionB: The choice cannot be made responsibly yet; what the workload spends its time on is what decides it
optionC: Buy the memory, since it is more flexible
optionD: Split the budget evenly between the two
correctAnswerText: The choice cannot be made responsibly yet; what the workload spends its time on is what decides it
explanation: Which component matters is a property of the work rather than of the machine, so an unknown workload leaves the question genuinely open. Splitting evenly is a way of avoiding the decision rather than making it.

prompt: A configuration is chosen for a workload and the workload later changes character entirely. What does that say about the original decision?
optionA: It was wrong, since the configuration no longer suits the work
optionB: It was right, and the workload should be changed back
optionC: It says nothing, since hardware decisions cannot be judged
optionD: It may have been right when it was made; a decision is judged on what was known then, and the configuration should now be revisited
correctAnswerText: It may have been right when it was made; a decision is judged on what was known then, and the configuration should now be revisited
explanation: A choice made well on the information available can be overtaken by events, and treating that as an error discourages making any decision at all. What follows is a fresh decision rather than a verdict on the old one.

prompt: A workload reads one small table over and over while streaming a very large file past it once. The table is far smaller than memory and the file is far larger. Which layer does the work depend on most?
optionA: Memory, to hold the small table, while the large file is read from storage as it goes
optionB: Storage, since the file dominates the data volume
optionC: Registers, since the table is small
optionD: Cache alone, since the table is read repeatedly
correctAnswerText: Memory, to hold the small table, while the large file is read from storage as it goes
explanation: The two parts of the workload have different needs and each lands on a different layer. The table is what is read repeatedly and must therefore be held close; the file is read once and has nowhere else to be.

prompt: A workload holds a dataset slightly larger than the machine's memory and touches all of it constantly. The processor is idle much of the time. Which layer decides how fast it runs?
optionA: The processor, since it does the work
optionB: Registers, since every value passes through them
optionC: Storage, because the part that will not fit is fetched from there again and again
optionD: Memory, since the dataset is nearly small enough to fit
correctAnswerText: Storage, because the part that will not fit is fetched from there again and again
explanation: Being slightly too large is the worst case: almost everything fits, and the small remainder is fetched from the slowest layer constantly. An idle processor confirms the wait is elsewhere.

prompt: A dataset just fits in memory, and it then grows by a few per cent. Performance falls off a cliff rather than degrading gently. Why?
optionA: Memory becomes slower as it fills
optionB: The part that no longer fits is fetched from storage repeatedly, and storage is far slower rather than slightly slower
optionC: The processor throttles itself when memory is full
optionD: The growth was larger than reported
correctAnswerText: The part that no longer fits is fetched from storage repeatedly, and storage is far slower rather than slightly slower
explanation: The layers differ by large factors rather than small ones, so crossing from one to the next is a step rather than a slope. A few per cent more data can move a large share of the accesses to a layer orders of magnitude slower.

prompt: A colleague suggests that keeping data in the fastest available layer is always the right choice. When does that advice fail?
optionA: Never; faster is always better
optionB: Whenever the data is read only once, since speed is wasted
optionC: Whenever the data must survive a restart, since fast layers are less reliable
optionD: Whenever the data does not fit; a layer that is faster and too small does not hold the data at all
correctAnswerText: Whenever the data does not fit; a layer that is faster and too small does not hold the data at all
explanation: Capacity is a constraint rather than a preference, so the fastest layer is only a candidate if the data fits in it. Reading data once is a weaker objection — speed still helps, it simply helps less.

prompt: An array holds 40, 55, 62, 77. What value is at position 0?
optionD: There is no position 0
explanation: Positions are counted from zero, so position 0 holds the first value. Counting from one would give the second value instead.

prompt: An array holds red, green, blue, white, black. At what position is white?
explanation: Counting red as position 0 puts white at position 3. Answering 4 counts from one, which is the commonest source of an off-by-one fault later.

prompt: An array holds 9, 4, 7, 1, 6. What value is at the last valid position?
optionD: There is no last position until the array is full
explanation: The last valid position holds the final value, which is 6. Answering 1 stops one position short, and 5 reports how many values there are rather than any of them.

prompt: An array holds 3 values. Which of these is a valid position?
explanation: Three values occupy positions 0, 1 and 2, so 1 is inside the array and 3 is one past the end. Using the count as a position is the single commonest array fault.

prompt: A collection holds 10, 20, 30, and a program reads the value at position 1. What does it get?
explanation: Counting from zero makes position 1 the second value, which is 20. Answering 10 counts from one, and 1 reports the position rather than what is stored there.

prompt: An array holds 6 values. What is its last valid position?
explanation: Six values occupy positions 0 to 5, so the last is one below the count. Treating the length as a position reads one past the end.

prompt: An array occupies positions 0 to 8. How many values does it hold?
explanation: Positions 0 to 8 inclusive is 9 positions, because the count includes both ends. Subtracting the two numbers gives 8 and forgets that both ends are occupied.

prompt: An array holds no values at all. What is its length?
optionB: Undefined
optionD: It cannot exist
explanation: An empty array is a perfectly ordinary array whose length is zero. It has no valid positions at all, which is different from having one.

prompt: Someone says an array's length and its last valid position are the same number. When is that true?
optionA: Always; both count the items
optionB: Never; the last position is always one below the length
optionC: When the array holds exactly one item
optionD: When the array is empty
correctAnswerText: Never; the last position is always one below the length
explanation: Counting from zero puts the two exactly one apart for every array. A single item gives length 1 and last position 0, and an empty array has length 0 and no valid position at all.

prompt: A value already stored at a position is changed to a different value. What is the operation, and does the length change?
optionA: Inserting, and the length increases by one
optionB: Removing, and the length decreases by one
optionC: Searching, and the length does not change
optionD: Replacing, and the length does not change
correctAnswerText: Replacing, and the length does not change
explanation: Replacing puts a new value where one already was, so nothing is added or lost. The length is what separates replacing from inserting.

prompt: A new value is put into the middle of an array without any existing value being lost. What is the operation, and does the length change?
optionA: Inserting, and the length increases by one
optionB: Replacing, and the length does not change
optionC: Inserting, and the length does not change
optionD: Removing, and the length decreases by one
correctAnswerText: Inserting, and the length increases by one
explanation: Nothing being lost means nothing was overwritten, so the array must have grown. An insertion that did not change the length would have to have destroyed something.

prompt: An array is examined to find whether a value is present. What happens to the array?
optionA: The found value is removed
optionB: The array is reordered so the value comes first
optionC: Nothing; searching reads and does not change anything
optionD: The length decreases by one
correctAnswerText: Nothing; searching reads and does not change anything
explanation: A search reports where something is, or that it is absent, and leaves the data as it found it. An operation that changed the array while looking would make repeated searches unreliable.

prompt: A value is removed from the middle of an array. What happens to the position it occupied?
optionA: The position is left empty and the length is unchanged
optionB: The later items move down to close the gap, and the length decreases by one
optionC: The position is filled with zero and the length is unchanged
optionD: The later items keep their positions and the length decreases by one
correctAnswerText: The later items move down to close the gap, and the length decreases by one
explanation: An array holds its items in consecutive positions, so removing one means everything after it moves. A gap left behind would break the rule that positions run without interruption.

prompt: An array holds 5, 8, 12, 20. The value 9 is inserted at position 1. What does the array hold?
explanation: The new value takes position 1 and everything from there onward moves up one place, so nothing is lost. Overwriting the 8 would be replacing rather than inserting.

prompt: An array holds 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. The value at position 1 is removed. Where is 15 afterwards?
optionA: Position 2
optionB: Position 3, where it was
optionC: Position 4
optionD: Position 1
correctAnswerText: Position 2
explanation: Removing an item moves everything after it down one place, so 15 falls from position 3 to position 2. Items keeping their old positions is what an array cannot do.

prompt: A collection holds 4, 9, 2, 7, 5. A traversal counts how many values exceed 4. What is the result?
explanation: The values 9, 7 and 5 exceed 4, so the count is 3. Answering 21 totals those values instead, and 4 counts the values that are 4 or more.

prompt: A collection holds -8, -3, -12, -5. A traversal finds the largest value, starting from the first item. What is the result?
explanation: Comparing each value against the running largest gives -3, which is the greatest of the four. Answering 0 is what a traversal starting from zero rather than from the first item would report — a value that never appears in the data.

prompt: An unsorted array holds 6, 2, 9, 4, 7. A search checks each item in turn for the value 9. How many comparisons does it make?
explanation: The search checks 6, then 2, then 9, stopping when it matches, which is 3 comparisons. Answering 2 gives the position rather than the number of comparisons.

prompt: An unsorted array of 20 items is searched for a value that is present as the very last item. How many comparisons does a check-each-in-turn search make?
explanation: Every item is checked, including the last, so the count equals the length of 20. Answering 19 stops one short, and 10 assumes an average rather than this particular case.

prompt: An unsorted array of 20 items is searched for a value that is not present at all. Someone says the search stops early because there is nothing to find. How many comparisons are made?
optionA: 19, since the last item need not be checked
optionB: 1, since the search stops as soon as it fails
optionC: 20; every item must be checked before absence can be established
optionD: 0, since the value is not there to compare against
correctAnswerText: 20; every item must be checked before absence can be established
explanation: Absence can only be established by exhausting the array, so the absent case costs the most rather than the least. Nothing in an unsorted array allows an earlier conclusion.

prompt: A sorted array holds 2, 5, 9, 14, 20, 27, 31. The middle value 14 is compared with a target of 27. Which items remain in consideration?
explanation: The target is larger than the middle, so everything at or below the middle is discarded and the upper part remains. Discarding from the wrong side would throw away the item being sought.

prompt: A sorted array holds 64 items. At most how many comparisons does a halving search need?
explanation: Each comparison halves what remains — 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 — which is 7 steps to reach a single item. Halving the length once gives 32, which is what one halving leaves rather than the number of steps.

prompt: A halving search is applied to an unsorted array of 100 items and reports that a value is absent. The value is in fact present. The search itself was implemented correctly. What is wrong?
optionA: The method requires the data to be in order, and discarding half of unsorted data discards it arbitrarily
optionB: The array is too large for a halving search
optionC: The search should have made more comparisons
optionD: The value must have been in a position the search cannot reach
correctAnswerText: The method requires the data to be in order, and discarding half of unsorted data discards it arbitrarily
explanation: Every step assumes that everything on the discarded side is smaller or larger, and unsorted data gives no such guarantee. A correct implementation of a method whose precondition fails is still wrong.

prompt: An array holds 5, 1, 4, 2. A pass compares each adjacent pair from the left and swaps them when the left is larger. What does the array hold after one complete pass?
explanation: The largest value is carried to the end by successive swaps while the rest move down one place. Answering the fully sorted array reports the eventual outcome rather than the state after one pass.

prompt: Continuing from 1, 4, 2, 5, a second pass of the same method runs. What does the array hold afterwards?
explanation: The second pass swaps 4 and 2 and leaves the rest, which happens to complete the ordering here. That it finishes early is a property of this data rather than of the method.

prompt: After one pass of the same method over an array of 6 items, someone says nothing useful has been achieved because the array is still unsorted. What has in fact been guaranteed?
optionA: The smallest item is now at the front
optionB: The array is half sorted
optionC: Nothing at all is guaranteed after a single pass
optionD: The largest item is now in its final position at the end
correctAnswerText: The largest item is now in its final position at the end
explanation: Each pass carries the largest remaining item all the way to the end, so one item is settled even when the rest look unchanged. That is exactly why later passes can examine one fewer item each time.

prompt: Reading the value at a stated position in an array of 10 items, and doing the same in an array of 10,000. Which does more work?
optionA: Neither; a position is reached directly, whatever the size
optionB: The larger array, since there is more to search through
optionC: The smaller array, since it is held differently
optionD: It cannot be said without knowing the values
correctAnswerText: Neither; a position is reached directly, whatever the size
explanation: An array reaches a position by calculation rather than by looking through the items, so the size does not enter into it. That is the property that makes an array worth using.

prompt: Inserting an item at the end of an array, and inserting one at the front. Which does more work as the array grows?
optionA: At the end, because the array may have to grow
optionB: Neither; both are a single operation
optionC: At the front, because every existing item has to move up one place
optionD: At the front, but only for arrays of more than a hundred items
correctAnswerText: At the front, because every existing item has to move up one place
explanation: Inserting at the front shifts every item, so the work rises with the length; at the end nothing has to move. Both being one line of code is what makes the difference invisible in the source.

prompt: A program builds a list by inserting each new item at the front, and becomes dramatically slower as the list grows. Each insertion is a single statement and the code is unchanged throughout. What accounts for it?
optionA: The statement is being executed more slowly as memory fills
optionB: Each insertion moves every item already present, so the work per insertion grows with the list
optionC: The insertions are correct but the list has grown too large to hold
optionD: Inserting is inherently slow regardless of position
correctAnswerText: Each insertion moves every item already present, so the work per insertion grows with the list
explanation: Unchanging code that gets slower as the data grows points at work that depends on the data rather than at the statement. Inserting at the end would show no such effect, which is what makes the position the cause.

prompt: A loop over an array of 5 items runs from position 0 up to and including position 5. What does the last pass do?
optionA: It reads the last item a second time
optionB: It reads nothing and the loop ends
optionC: It wraps around and reads the first item
optionD: It reads a position that is not part of the array
correctAnswerText: It reads a position that is not part of the array
explanation: Five items occupy positions 0 to 4, so position 5 is past the end. Nothing wraps around, and the pass does happen — which is why the fault is not simply an ignored extra step.

prompt: The same loop bound is used in two languages: one reports an error on the last pass and the other returns whatever is in that memory. What does that difference reflect?
optionA: Whether the language checks the position before using it
optionB: Whether the array was declared with a fixed size
optionC: Whether the loop counts from zero
optionD: Whether the array holds numbers or text
correctAnswerText: Whether the language checks the position before using it
explanation: The fault is identical in both; what differs is whether anything is watching for it. A checked language turns a silent wrong answer into a stopped program, which is a difference in what happens rather than in what was written.

prompt: A total computed over an array is slightly too large, and the amount by which it is wrong changes between runs. Every value in the array is correct and the addition is correct. What is wrong?
optionA: One of the values is being added twice
optionB: The total is not initialised before the loop
optionC: The loop reads one position past the end and adds whatever happens to be there
optionD: The array has grown since it was created
correctAnswerText: The loop reads one position past the end and adds whatever happens to be there
explanation: A varying error with correct data and correct arithmetic points at something outside the array being included. An uninitialised total would give an error that varies too, but it would rarely be slight, and adding a value twice would give the same error every run.

prompt: An array holds A, B, C, D, E. One position starts at the front and one at the back; they swap their values and then move toward each other. What does the array hold after two swaps?
optionA: E, B, C, D, A
optionB: E, D, C, B, A
optionC: A, D, C, B, E
optionD: E, D, C, A, B
correctAnswerText: E, D, C, B, A
explanation: The first swap exchanges the ends and the second exchanges the pair inside them, leaving the middle alone. Two swaps is enough to reverse five items, because the middle item has nowhere to go.

prompt: A reversal using two positions moving toward each other is run on an array of 6 items and the array comes back exactly as it started. The swap itself is correct and both positions do move. What is wrong?
optionA: The swap is being applied to the same position twice
optionB: The array has an even number of items, which the method cannot handle
optionC: The positions are moving in the same direction
optionD: The positions continue past each other, so every swap is performed a second time and undone
correctAnswerText: The positions continue past each other, so every swap is performed a second time and undone
explanation: Every pair being swapped twice returns the array to its original state, which is what running past the crossing point produces. An even count is handled perfectly well when the loop stops at the crossing.

prompt: Marks for 60 students must be stored so that any one of them can be reached by its position. Which arrangement fits?
optionA: One array of 60 values, reached by position
optionB: Sixty separate variables, one per student
optionC: One value holding all sixty marks together
optionD: One array holding only the highest mark
correctAnswerText: One array of 60 values, reached by position
explanation: Reaching a value by position is exactly what an array offers, and it works whatever the count. Sixty separate names cannot be reached by a computed position and would have to be written out individually.

prompt: A value must be found once in an unsorted array of 1,000 items. Someone proposes sorting the array first and then using a halving search. The proposal would give the correct answer. Is it a good choice?
optionA: Yes; a halving search is always faster than checking each item
optionB: Yes; sorted data is always preferable
optionC: No; sorting costs far more than the single traversal it saves, and the array is used only once
optionD: No; a halving search cannot be used on data that was sorted afterwards
correctAnswerText: No; sorting costs far more than the single traversal it saves, and the array is used only once
explanation: The proposal is correct and the question is cost. Sorting a thousand items to save one traversal of a thousand items loses; had many searches been needed, the same proposal would win.

prompt: A traversal reports a total that is always short by exactly the first value. What is the fault?
optionA: The loop ends one position early
optionB: The loop begins at position 1 rather than position 0
optionC: The total is initialised inside the loop
optionD: The values are being read in reverse
correctAnswerText: The loop begins at position 1 rather than position 0
explanation: Being short by exactly the first item points at where the loop starts. Ending early would omit the last item instead, and initialising inside the loop would leave only the final value.

prompt: A traversal reports a total short by exactly the last value. The loop starts at position 0 and the addition is correct. What is the fault?
optionA: The loop starts one position too late
optionB: The last value is being read as zero
optionC: The total is initialised to the first value
optionD: The loop stops one position before the end
correctAnswerText: The loop stops one position before the end
explanation: Which end the missing value came from identifies which bound is wrong, and the stem rules the start out. Initialising to the first value would give a total that is too large rather than too small.

prompt: A traversal finding the largest value reports 0 for an array in which every value is negative, and reports correctly for every array containing a positive value. What is the fault, and why did it survive testing?
optionA: The running largest starts at 0, which no negative value beats; every test array happened to contain something positive
optionB: The comparison is reversed, and the test arrays were sorted
optionC: The loop skips negative values, and the test arrays had none
optionD: The array cannot hold negative values, and the tests avoided them
correctAnswerText: The running largest starts at 0, which no negative value beats; every test array happened to contain something positive
explanation: A value appears in the output that is not in the data, which places the fault in the starting value rather than in the comparison. Testing found nothing because a single positive value in an array hides the fault completely.

prompt: Two candidate starting values for a largest-value traversal are proposed: zero, and the first item of the array. Which is correct, and what does the other require?
optionA: Zero, because it is smaller than any value that could appear
optionB: Either; both give the same answer on any array
optionC: The first item; starting from zero is only safe if the data is guaranteed to contain a positive value
optionD: Zero, provided the array is checked for negatives first
correctAnswerText: The first item; starting from zero is only safe if the data is guaranteed to contain a positive value
explanation: A starting value taken from the data can never be beaten by the data being unusual, which is why it needs no guarantee. Zero imposes a condition on the input that nothing in the code states or checks.

prompt: An array fault produces a slightly wrong total, and another produces a wildly wrong one. Which is more likely to reach production, and why?
optionA: The wild one, because large numbers are harder to notice
optionB: The slight one, because a plausible total passes the informal checks people actually make
optionC: They are equally likely, since both are faults
optionD: The slight one, because small errors are harder to fix
correctAnswerText: The slight one, because a plausible total passes the informal checks people actually make
explanation: What keeps a fault alive is not its size but whether anybody questions the output. A total that looks about right is accepted; one that is obviously absurd is investigated the first time it appears.

prompt: An approach compares each item with the one after it. It behaves correctly on every array of two or more items that it has been given. Which input breaks it?
optionA: An array of two items, where only one comparison is possible
optionB: An array with repeated values
optionC: An array in reverse order
optionD: An array of exactly one item, where there is no following item to compare with
correctAnswerText: An array of exactly one item, where there is no following item to compare with
explanation: Reading ahead by one needs a successor to exist, and only a single item leaves none. Two items give exactly one comparison, which is the smallest case that works rather than the smallest that fails.

prompt: An approach compares each item with the one after it. What does it produce for an empty array?
optionA: Nothing, and correctly so; there are no pairs and the loop runs zero times
optionB: A failure, because there is no first item to read
optionC: A single comparison against nothing
optionD: The same result as for a single item
correctAnswerText: Nothing, and correctly so; there are no pairs and the loop runs zero times
explanation: With no items there is nothing to start from either, so the loop never begins and no access is attempted. Empty and single-item input fail in different ways here, which is why both are worth trying.

prompt: A search reports the position of a value. What should it report when the value is absent, and why not simply zero?
optionA: Zero, which is the natural empty answer
optionB: The length of the array, which is always safe
optionC: Something no valid position can be, since zero is itself a valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front
optionD: Nothing; it should stop with an error instead
correctAnswerText: Something no valid position can be, since zero is itself a valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front
explanation: Counting from zero means the first position and the "not found" answer would collide, so the value has to lie outside the range of positions. Being absent is an expected outcome rather than a fault, so stopping is too strong.

prompt: A reversal using two positions moving toward each other is run on an array of exactly one item. What happens?
optionA: The item is swapped with itself and lost
optionB: Nothing; the two positions already meet, so no swap is performed and the array is correct
optionC: The method fails, because there is no pair to swap
optionD: The positions cross immediately and the loop runs endlessly
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the two positions already meet, so no swap is performed and the array is correct
explanation: The stopping condition is already satisfied before any swap, so the loop does no work — and doing no work is exactly right for reversing one item. An edge case that needs no special handling is worth recognising as such.

prompt: An approach is correct for arrays of two or more items and wrong for one item. Two fixes are proposed: add a special case for a single item, or change the loop bound so the single-item case falls out correctly. Which is preferable?
optionA: The special case, because it leaves the working behaviour untouched
optionB: Either; both produce the right answer
optionC: The special case, because loop bounds are harder to reason about
optionD: Changing the bound where it works, since a special case is another path that must stay correct as the code changes
correctAnswerText: Changing the bound where it works, since a special case is another path that must stay correct as the code changes
explanation: Both fix the symptom and they leave different things behind. A bound that handles every size needs no upkeep; a special case has to be remembered by everyone who edits the code afterwards.

prompt: A collection is searched thousands of times a day and added to twice a day. Both keeping it sorted and leaving it unsorted would work. Which arrangement suits it?
optionA: Keep it sorted, since the cost falls on the rare operation and the frequent one becomes much cheaper
optionB: Leave it unsorted, since sorting costs more than searching
optionC: Leave it unsorted, since insertions must stay fast
optionD: Either; the usage pattern does not affect the choice
correctAnswerText: Keep it sorted, since the cost falls on the rare operation and the frequent one becomes much cheaper
explanation: The usage decides it: sorting is paid twice a day and repaid thousands of times. The same two arrangements would be ranked the other way round if the frequencies were reversed.

prompt: A collection is added to constantly and searched once a week. Which arrangement suits it, and what does the choice cost?
optionA: Keep it sorted, so the weekly search is fast
optionB: Keep it sorted, since sorted data is always preferable
optionC: Leave it unsorted; the weekly search costs a full traversal, which is far less than keeping every insertion in order
optionD: Either; a weekly search is too rare to matter
correctAnswerText: Leave it unsorted; the weekly search costs a full traversal, which is far less than keeping every insertion in order
explanation: Reversing the frequencies reverses the answer, which is the point: the cost of order is paid on every insertion, and here insertions are what dominate. The weekly traversal is a real cost and a small one.

prompt: A collection is both added to and searched constantly, in roughly equal measure. What follows about the choice between sorted and unsorted?
optionA: Sorted, since searching is the more important operation
optionB: Neither arrangement is clearly better, and the answer depends on measuring the two costs rather than reasoning about them
optionC: Unsorted, since insertion is the more frequent operation
optionD: Sorted, since a tie should be broken in favour of order
correctAnswerText: Neither arrangement is clearly better, and the answer depends on measuring the two costs rather than reasoning about them
explanation: The rule that decides the two lopsided cases gives no answer when neither dominates, and inventing a tiebreak dresses a guess as a principle. Recognising where a rule stops applying is part of using it.

prompt: A team keeps a collection sorted so that searches are fast, and later discovers that almost all the searches are for the most recently added item. What does that change?
optionA: Nothing; sorted data is faster to search whatever is being sought
optionB: The ordering becomes more valuable, since recent items are at one end
optionC: The collection should be sorted in the opposite direction
optionD: The ordering buys much less than expected, since the newest item could be found immediately without it
correctAnswerText: The ordering buys much less than expected, since the newest item could be found immediately without it
explanation: A cost decision rests on what the operations actually are, and "search" turned out to mean something narrower than assumed. Sorting by value does not put the newest item anywhere in particular, so reversing the order does not help either.

prompt: The text is "my code". What character is at position 0?
optionA: y
optionB: m
optionC: c
optionD: There is no position 0
correctAnswerText: m
explanation: Positions are counted from zero, so the first character sits at position 0. Counting from one would give the second character instead.

prompt: The text is "my code". What character is at position 2?
optionA: c
optionB: y
optionC: o
optionD: A space
correctAnswerText: A space
explanation: A space is a character like any other and occupies its own position, so it sits between the two words at position 2. Skipping it shifts every later position by one.

prompt: The text is "my code". At what position is the letter c?
explanation: Counting m as 0, y as 1 and the space as 2 puts c at position 3. Answering 2 is what ignoring the space produces.

prompt: The text is "go now". What is at the last valid position?
optionA: o
optionB: A space
optionC: w
optionD: There is none until the text is complete
correctAnswerText: w
explanation: The last valid position holds the final character, which is w. Answering o stops one short, which is what treating the length as the last position and then correcting twice produces.

prompt: The text is "a b c", with single spaces between the letters. How many positions does it occupy, and what is at position 1?
optionA: Three positions, and position 1 holds b
optionB: Five positions, and position 1 holds a space
optionC: Five positions, and position 1 holds b
optionD: Three positions, and position 1 holds a space
correctAnswerText: Five positions, and position 1 holds a space
explanation: Three letters and two spaces occupy five positions in all, and the first space follows the first letter. Counting only the letters gives three and moves every later character.

prompt: What is the length of the text "data set"?
explanation: Seven letters and one space make a length of 8. Answering 7 omits the space, and 2 counts the words rather than the characters.

prompt: What is the length of the text "hi " — the two letters followed by a single trailing space?
explanation: A trailing space is a character and is counted, so the length is three. It is invisible when the text is displayed, which is exactly why it is missed.

prompt: What is the length of text containing no characters at all?
optionB: Undefined
optionD: It cannot exist
explanation: Empty text is ordinary text whose length is zero, and it has no valid positions. That is different from text containing a single space, whose length is one.

prompt: A program holds the text "career" and reports its length. What is reported?
optionD: career
explanation: Six characters give a length of 6. Answering 5 or 7 is off by one at an end, and reporting the text itself answers a different question.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text "Yes" and "yes" compare as equal?
optionA: Yes; they spell the same word
optionB: Yes; comparison ignores case
optionC: It cannot be decided without knowing the language
optionD: No; the first characters differ
correctAnswerText: No; the first characters differ
explanation: A comparison examines the characters, and an upper-case letter is a different character from its lower-case form. Spelling the same word is not the same as being the same text.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text "OK" and "OK" compare as equal?
optionA: Yes; every character matches
optionB: No; identical text never compares equal
optionC: Yes, but only if the two are stored in the same place
optionD: It depends on how the text was created
correctAnswerText: Yes; every character matches
explanation: Comparison is about the characters and nothing else, so identical characters compare equal however each piece of text came to exist.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text " ok" and "ok" compare as equal — the first with a single leading space?
optionA: Yes; a leading space is ignored
optionB: Yes; both contain the same letters
optionC: No; the first has an extra character at the front
optionD: No; the two have the same length but differ in case
correctAnswerText: No; the first has an extra character at the front
explanation: A leading space is a character, so the two pieces differ in both length and content. Nothing strips spaces on the way into a comparison.

prompt: A program compares a typed answer with the stored answer "Blue" and rejects "blue" as wrong. What change would accept both?
optionA: Compare the lengths instead of the characters
optionB: Convert both to the same case before comparing
optionC: Store the answer in lower case only
optionD: Nothing; the two are genuinely different answers
correctAnswerText: Convert both to the same case before comparing
explanation: Bringing both sides to a common case removes the distinction before the comparison sees it. Storing the answer in lower case alone would still reject a capitalised entry.

prompt: The text is "abcdef". A range starts at position 1 and stops before position 4. What does it produce?
optionA: bcde
optionB: abcd
optionC: bc
optionD: bcd
correctAnswerText: bcd
explanation: Positions 1, 2 and 3 are taken and position 4 is not, because the range stops before it. Including the end gives one character too many.

prompt: The text is "network". A range starts at position 3 and stops before position 3. What does it produce?
optionA: Nothing; the range is empty
optionB: w
optionC: wo
optionD: The whole text
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the range is empty
explanation: A range that starts where it stops contains no positions at all, so the result is empty. That is a legitimate outcome rather than an error, and it is what an off-by-one in the wrong direction quietly produces.

prompt: A variable holds "Report". An operation converting it to upper case is performed, and its result is not stored anywhere. What does the variable hold afterwards?
optionA: REPORT
optionB: report
optionC: Report
optionD: Nothing; the value was consumed
correctAnswerText: Report
explanation: The operation builds new text and hands it back, leaving the original untouched. Discarding the result therefore changes nothing at all.

prompt: A variable holds " total " with a space at each end. A trimming operation is applied and its result is assigned to a second variable. What do the two variables hold?
optionA: Both hold "total"
optionB: The first still holds " total " and the second holds "total"
optionC: The first holds "total" and the second holds " total "
optionD: Both hold " total "
correctAnswerText: The first still holds " total " and the second holds "total"
explanation: Trimming produces new text and the original is unchanged, so the two variables differ. Assigning the result is what makes the trimmed version available at all.

prompt: The text is "banana". A search for "an" reports the position of the first match. What does it report?
explanation: The first "an" begins at position 1, counting b as 0. Position 3 is where the second match begins, which is what reporting the last match would give.

prompt: The text is "banana". A search for "xy" is performed. What should the result be?
optionA: A value that is not a valid position, marking absence
optionB: 0, since nothing was found
optionC: The length of the text
optionD: An error, since the search failed
correctAnswerText: A value that is not a valid position, marking absence
explanation: Zero is a perfectly valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front, so absence has to be reported by something outside the range of positions. Not finding something is an ordinary outcome rather than a failure.

prompt: A program treats a search result of 0 as meaning "not found" and reports that a value is missing when it is actually the first thing in the text. The search itself returns the correct position. What is wrong?
optionA: The search is returning the wrong position
optionB: The value being searched for is empty
optionC: Zero is a real position, so it cannot also stand for absence
optionD: The text has a leading space, shifting the position
correctAnswerText: Zero is a real position, so it cannot also stand for absence
explanation: The search is stated to be correct, so the fault is in how its answer is read. A match at the very front is the one case where a valid position collides with the marker chosen for absence.

prompt: The text "red,green,blue" is split on the comma. How many pieces result?
explanation: Two separators divide the text into three pieces. The count of pieces is always one more than the count of separators when none of them sit at an end.

prompt: A line ends with the separator it uses: "north;south;" split on the semicolon. What is the final piece?
optionA: south, because a trailing separator is ignored
optionB: A semicolon, because the separator is kept
optionC: There is no final piece; the split yields two
optionD: An empty piece, following the last semicolon
correctAnswerText: An empty piece, following the last semicolon
explanation: A separator at the end still separates, so something follows it and that something is empty. The separator itself never appears inside any piece.

prompt: The text "a,,b" is split on the comma and a program reports two pieces. It expects one piece per value and the two commas are genuinely present in the data. What has it done wrong?
optionA: It has discarded the empty piece between the two commas, which the split produces
optionB: It has treated the two commas as one separator, which is correct
optionC: It has included the comma in one of the pieces
optionD: It has split on the wrong character
correctAnswerText: It has discarded the empty piece between the two commas, which the split produces
explanation: Consecutive separators produce an empty piece between them, so the split gives three. A program reporting two has dropped it, which loses the information that a value was missing there.

prompt: The pieces red, green and blue are joined with a comma between them. What is produced?
optionA: red,green,blue,
optionB: ,red,green,blue
optionC: red,green,blue
optionD: redgreenblue
correctAnswerText: red,green,blue
explanation: Separators go between pieces, so three pieces need two separators and none at either end. A trailing separator is what building the text piece by piece without care produces.

prompt: Five pieces are joined with a separator between them. How many separators appear?
explanation: Separators sit in the gaps between pieces, and five pieces have 4 gaps. Answering 5 places one after the last piece as well.

prompt: A program builds a list by adding each value followed by a comma, and the result always ends with a stray comma. Every value is present and in the right order. What is the smallest change that fixes it?
optionA: Remove the last value as well as the comma
optionB: Add the values in reverse order
optionC: Use a different separator character
optionD: Put the separator before each value except the first, rather than after each value
correctAnswerText: Put the separator before each value except the first, rather than after each value
explanation: Every value being correct places the fault in where the separator goes rather than in the data. Moving it to precede each value except the first gives exactly one separator per gap and none at either end.

prompt: Two entries display as "cat" and "cat", and a comparison reports them as different. The second has a trailing space. Why do they not match?
optionA: The second contains one more character than the first
optionB: The two differ in case
optionC: The two have the same length and differ in content
optionD: A comparison cannot be relied on for text
correctAnswerText: The second contains one more character than the first
explanation: A trailing space is a character that shows as nothing, so the two pieces differ in length while looking identical. Nothing about the comparison is unreliable.

prompt: Two entries both display as "no data" and both are seven characters long, yet they do not match. One uses a single space and the other uses a different invisible character of the same width. What is the cause?
optionA: One of them has a trailing space
optionB: The two differ in case somewhere
optionC: The invisible characters differ, so the two are different text of the same length
optionD: Equal-length text always matches, so the report is wrong
correctAnswerText: The invisible characters differ, so the two are different text of the same length
explanation: Equal length rules out a missing or extra character, and identical appearance rules out a visible difference — which leaves a character that is invisible and not the one expected. Length is a weaker check than it looks.

prompt: A lookup fails for entries typed by hand and succeeds for the same entries loaded from a file. The values look identical in both cases and the lookup itself is correct. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The typed entries differ in case
optionB: The typed entries carry leading or trailing spaces that the file entries do not
optionC: The lookup is case-sensitive and the file is not
optionD: The file entries were converted to a different format
correctAnswerText: The typed entries carry leading or trailing spaces that the file entries do not
explanation: Identical appearance with different behaviour, split cleanly by how the value arrived, points at something invisible that typing adds. Case would be visible in the comparison, and the lookup is stated to be correct.

prompt: A traversal counts the vowels in "open air". How many does it find?
explanation: The vowels are o, e, a and i, giving a count of 4. The space is not a vowel and the consonants are not counted, so 8 reports the length instead.

prompt: A traversal counts characters in "go on" that are not spaces. How many does it find?
explanation: Five positions hold four letters and one space, so the count excluding spaces is 4. Answering 5 counts everything, which is the length rather than the count asked for.

prompt: A traversal building a reversed copy of "abc" produces "cba" correctly, and on "ab c" it produces "c ba". The traversal visits every position exactly once. Is that correct?
optionA: No; the space should have stayed where it was
optionB: No; the space should have been removed
optionC: Yes; reversing includes the space, and "c ba" is the reverse of "ab c"
optionD: No; the words should have been reversed rather than the characters
correctAnswerText: Yes; reversing includes the space, and "c ba" is the reverse of "ab c"
explanation: Reversing the characters moves every one of them, the space included, and the result is exactly what that gives. Expecting the space to stay put confuses reversing the characters with reversing the words.

prompt: A check compares the first character with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on, treating case as significant and spaces as characters. Does "Level" pass?
optionA: Yes; the letters read the same in both directions
optionB: No; the first character is upper case and the last is lower case
optionC: No; the text has an odd number of characters
optionD: Yes; case is ignored in a symmetry check
correctAnswerText: No; the first character is upper case and the last is lower case
explanation: The stem states that case is significant, and L does not match l. Reading the word as symmetric requires ignoring exactly the thing the check is told to respect.

prompt: The same check is applied to "abcba", comparing from both ends inward. It reports success after 2 comparisons. Someone expects 5. Why is 2 correct?
optionA: The check stops as soon as it finds one match
optionB: The check compares only the outermost pair
optionC: The count should be 5; the report is wrong
optionD: Each comparison settles two characters, and the middle character needs none
correctAnswerText: Each comparison settles two characters, and the middle character needs none
explanation: Five characters form two pairs with one left in the middle, and a character compared with itself proves nothing. Expecting one comparison per character double-counts every pair.

prompt: Text is built by repeatedly adding one character to the end of existing text, producing new text each time. What happens to the work as the text grows?
optionA: It rises, because each addition copies everything built so far
optionB: It stays the same, since one character is added each time
optionC: It falls, since the text is already partly built
optionD: It stays the same, since the code is one line either way
correctAnswerText: It rises, because each addition copies everything built so far
explanation: Each addition produces new text containing everything that came before, so the copying grows with the length. That both approaches are one line of code is exactly why the difference is invisible in the source.

prompt: Two methods build the same text and produce identical results. One adds to existing text repeatedly and the other collects the pieces and joins them once at the end. Which does more work, and why?
optionA: The join, because it must examine every piece at the end
optionB: Neither; identical results mean identical work
optionC: The repeated addition, because every step copies what has already been built
optionD: The repeated addition, because it uses more lines of code
correctAnswerText: The repeated addition, because every step copies what has already been built
explanation: Identical results settle correctness and say nothing about cost. Collecting and joining once copies each piece a single time, while repeated addition copies the growing result again at every step.

prompt: A traversal over text produces output missing its final character. What is the fault?
optionA: The loop starts one position too late
optionB: The loop stops one position before the end
optionC: The output is being built in reverse
optionD: The final character is a space and was skipped
correctAnswerText: The loop stops one position before the end
explanation: Which end the missing character came from identifies which bound is wrong. Starting late would drop the first character instead.

prompt: A program builds a comma-separated list and the output ends with a comma but is otherwise correct. Every value appears exactly once and in order. What is the fault?
optionA: A separator is added before every value, including the first
optionB: The final value is missing and only its separator remains
optionC: The values are being joined in the wrong order
optionD: A separator is added after every value, including the last
correctAnswerText: A separator is added after every value, including the last
explanation: A trailing separator with every value present places the fault at the end rather than in the data. Adding the separator before each value would have produced a leading one instead, which is a distinguishable symptom.

prompt: Two faults produce similar-looking output: one drops the last character of the text, and one adds a trailing separator. How can they be told apart from the output alone?
optionA: One output is shorter than it should be and the other longer, and only the second ends in a separator
optionB: They cannot be told apart from the output alone
optionC: Only the first changes the length of the output
optionD: Only the second affects the order of the values
correctAnswerText: One output is shorter than it should be and the other longer, and only the second ends in a separator
explanation: Each fault leaves its own signature: a missing character shortens the result, and a stray separator lengthens it and is visible at the end. Reading the output carefully is what separates two faults that both look like an off-by-one.

prompt: A program strips spaces from the ends of every entry and a lookup still fails for one of them. What is the next thing to check, and why?
optionA: Whether the lookup is case-sensitive, since stripping does not affect case
optionB: Whether the entry is longer than the others, since length affects matching
optionC: Whether the entry contains an invisible character that is not a space, since stripping removes only what it recognises
optionD: Whether stripping was applied to both sides of the comparison
correctAnswerText: Whether the entry contains an invisible character that is not a space, since stripping removes only what it recognises
explanation: Stripping handles the spaces it knows about and leaves anything else, so an entry that still fails after stripping points at a character that looks like a space and is not. Case is worth checking too and would not have been masked by the stripping.

prompt: A text fault produces output that is obviously mangled, and another produces output that looks right and is subtly wrong. Which costs more, and why?
optionA: The mangled one, because more of the output is affected
optionB: The subtle one, because mangled output is noticed immediately while plausible output is used
optionC: They cost the same, since both are faults
optionD: The subtle one, because it is harder to reproduce
correctAnswerText: The subtle one, because mangled output is noticed immediately while plausible output is used
explanation: What limits the damage a fault does is whether anyone notices it. Obviously broken output is investigated the first time it appears; output that reads correctly travels onward and is acted on.

prompt: A symmetry check comparing from both ends inward is given empty text. It reports success without making any comparison. Is that correct?
optionA: No; it should have failed, since there is nothing to check
optionB: No; it should have stopped with an error
optionC: Yes, but only because the check does not handle empty text
optionD: Yes; empty text is trivially symmetric and there is nothing to compare
correctAnswerText: Yes; empty text is trivially symmetric and there is nothing to compare
explanation: The check reports failure only when a pair disagrees, and with no pairs there is no disagreement. Reporting success is the right answer rather than an accident of how the loop is written.

prompt: A traversal counting vowels is given empty text. What does it produce?
optionA: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
optionB: A failure, because there is nothing to examine
optionC: Nothing at all, because the loop never runs
optionD: An error, because the counter was never used
correctAnswerText: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
explanation: The loop runs zero times and the counter keeps the zero it started at, which is the right answer for counting nothing. The initialisation is what makes the empty case safe.

prompt: An approach reads the first character of text in order to decide something. What does it do on empty text?
optionA: It reads an empty character and continues
optionB: It returns without doing anything
optionC: It fails, because there is no first character to read
optionD: It reads a space, which stands in for the missing character
correctAnswerText: It fails, because there is no first character to read
explanation: Reading position 0 requires a character to be there, and empty text has none. Nothing substitutes a blank on the program's behalf, which is why this case has to be handled deliberately.

prompt: Splitting empty text on a comma produces how many pieces?
optionA: None
optionB: One, which is itself empty
optionC: Two, both empty
optionD: It fails, since there is nothing to split
correctAnswerText: One, which is itself empty
explanation: A split always produces one more piece than the separators it finds, and finding none gives one piece — the whole of the input, which happens to be empty. Answering none confuses an empty piece with no piece.

prompt: An approach works for text of two characters or more and fails for one character. Two fixes are proposed: a special case for single-character text, or a change to the loop bound. Which is preferable?
optionA: The special case, because it leaves working behaviour untouched
optionB: Either; both give the right answer
optionC: The special case, because bounds are harder to reason about
optionD: The bound, where it can be made to cover the case, since a special case is another path to keep correct
correctAnswerText: The bound, where it can be made to cover the case, since a special case is another path to keep correct
explanation: Both remove the symptom and they leave different things behind. A bound that handles every length needs no upkeep; a special case has to be remembered by everyone who edits the code afterwards.

prompt: Values must be extracted from lines where fields are separated by commas, and some fields are empty so consecutive commas occur. Which approach handles it?
optionA: Split on the comma and keep every piece, empty ones included
optionB: Split on the comma and discard empty pieces
optionC: Split on runs of commas, treating consecutive ones as one separator
optionD: Search for each field by position within the line
correctAnswerText: Split on the comma and keep every piece, empty ones included
explanation: Empty fields have to survive, or later fields shift into the wrong positions. Both of the discarding approaches work on tidy data and silently corrupt exactly the lines the stem describes.

prompt: Words must be counted in a line where words may be separated by more than one space. Which approach handles it?
optionA: Split on a single space and count the pieces
optionB: Count the spaces and add one
optionC: Split on runs of spaces, so that consecutive spaces produce no empty words
optionD: Count the characters and divide by the average word length
